Hemodynamic & Monitoring Set‑up | Monitor | How to place / what to watch | Frequency | |---------|------------------------------|-----------| | **Arterial line (radial)** – preferably **bilateral** (right & left) | Gives real‑time SBP/DBP, allows accurate titration of β‑blocker & nitroprusside; also detects inter‑arm pressure differences that may signal limb malperfusion. | Continuous; document every minute. | | **Central venous catheter (optional)** | Helpful for rapid fluid/vasopressor administration, central venous pressure (CVP) trending, and for later intra‑operative lines. | Continuous if placed. | | **12‑lead ECG** (continuous telemetry) | Detect new ST‑segment changes (coronary involvement), arrhythmias, high‑grade AV block (possible with proximal dissection). | Continuous. | | **Pulse oximetry & capnography** | Baseline oxygenation; early detection of respiratory compromise from AR or pulmonary edema. | Continuous. | | **Urine output (Foley)** | Goal ≥ 0.5 mL/kg/h; early sign of renal malperfusion. | Hourly. | | **Serial bedside TTE / TEE** | Re‑assess aortic valve function (new AR), pericardial effusion/tamponade, flap progression. Ideally a **focused TEE** in the OR prep area if available. | Every 30‑60 min or if clinical change. | | **Laboratory panel (stat)** | • CBC, BMP, Mg, PO4, lactate, ABG, coag profile, fibrinogen, D‑dimer, troponin, CK‑MB.
• Type‑and‑cross for possible blood transfusion. | Baseline, then q4‑6 h or as clinically indicated. | | **Neurologic checks** (NIHSS‑type) | Monitor for stroke or spinal cord ischemia (new weakness, change in mental status). | Every 15 min initially, then hourly. | | **Extremity perfusion** (pulse palpation, Doppler, temperature) | Detect limb malperfusion early. | Every 15 min. | --- ## 3. Key Considerations & “Pitfalls” in the Pre‑Operative Window | Issue | Why it matters | How to anticipate / mitigate | |-------|----------------|------------------------------| | **Propagation of the dissection** | Ongoing shear can extend proximally (affect coronary ostia) or distally (causing malperfusion). | Tight HR ≤ 60 bpm, SBP ≈ 110 mmHg, avoid reflex tachycardia. | | **Acute aortic regurgitation** (new diastolic murmur) | Can precipitate flash pulmonary edema. | Keep afterload low (nitroprusside), avoid excessive fluids, monitor lung fields & SpO₂, have CPAP/BiPAP ready. | | **Cardiac tamponade** (pericardial effusion) | Classic cause of sudden death. | Serial TTE/TEE, keep a low threshold for emergent pericardiocentesis if echo shows > 10 mm effusion with RV diastolic collapse. | | **Coronary artery involvement** (MI) | Dissection can occlude the right coronary or left main. | Continuous ECG; if ST‑elevation develops, treat as “type‑A dissection with MI” – do **NOT** give fibrinolytics; go straight to OR with cardiopulmonary bypass capability. | | **Cerebral malperfusion / stroke** | Dissection extending into carotid arteries. | Check neuro exam frequently; maintain MAP ≥ 60 mmHg but avoid hypertension that worsens cerebral edema. | | **Renal / mesenteric malperfusion** | False lumen can obstruct branch vessels → AKI, bowel ischemia. | Monitor urine output, lactate, abdominal pain; consider CTA of abdomen/pelvis if abdominal pain or rising lactate. | | **Spinal cord ischemia** | Rare but catastrophic. | Keep MAP ≥ 70 mmHg for the first few hours if any sign of lower‑extremity weakness; avoid profound hypotension. | | **Bleeding / coagulopathy** | Nitroprusside can cause cyanide toxicity (rare in short‑term) and can worsen bleeding if the patient is already coagulopathic. | Keep nitroprusside < 2 µg/kg/min for < 24 h; monitor lactate, methemoglobin if prolonged. Have cyanide antidote kit available (hydroxocobalamin). | | **Medication contraindications** | • **Asthma / severe COPD** – esmolol OK, labetalol may cause bronchospasm.
• **Severe aortic stenosis** – β‑blocker still needed, but avoid rapid afterload reduction. | Review past meds, allergies; if labetalol contraindicated, use esmolol + nicardipine instead of nitroprusside. | | **Pregnancy** (not applicable here) | Avoid teratogenic drugs; surgery still indicated. | N/A. | | **Logistics** | Operating‑room availability, cardiothoracic team, blood bank, ECMO backup. | Activate “aortic dissection pathway” early; keep OR on standby, have perfusionist on call, arrange for rapid transport (dedicated stretcher, portable monitor). | --- ## 4. Practical “Cheat‑Sheet” for the ED Nurse/Resident 1. **Analgesia** – Morphine 4 mg IV now, repeat q5 min until pain ≤ 3. 2. **β‑Blocker** – Esmolol 0.5 mg/kg bolus → start infusion 50 µg/kg/min; titrate to HR ≤ 60. 3. **Vasodilator** – Nitroprusside 0.3 µg/kg/min (add only after HR ≤ 60). Target SBP ≈ 110 mmHg. 4. **Arterial line** – Right radial (higher pressure) and left radial (lower pressure) ASAP. 5. **Labs** – CBC, BMP, coag, ABG, lactate, troponin, D‑dimer, type‑&‑cross. 6. **Imaging** – Bedside TTE already done; if TEE available, repeat after drug titration. CTA only if patient stabilizes and you need distal extent (rare before OR). 7. **Consults** – Cardiothoracic surgery, anesthesia, perfusion, ICU. 8. **Documentation** – Record all drug doses, infusion rates, vitals every 2 min, and any change in neurologic or perfusion status. --- ### Bottom line - **Control shear forces first**: β‑blocker → HR ≤ 60 bpm. - **Then lower pressure**: nitroprusside (or nicardipine) to SBP ≈ 110 mmHg (MAP ≈ 60‑70 mmHg). - **Pain control** = essential adjunct to hemodynamic control. - **Continuous, invasive monitoring** (bilateral arterial lines, telemetry, urine output, serial echo) is mandatory because the window to surgery is short and complications can evolve minute‑by‑minute. - **Never give anticoagulants or fibrinolytics**; any sign of tamponade or limb/organ malperfusion should trigger immediate surgical (or pericardiocentesis) action rather than medical “rescue”. Following this algorithm will keep the dissection from extending, buy you time for the operating room, and allow you to catch the most common life‑threatening complications before they become irreversible. *Stay calm, stay fast, keep the heart slow and the pressure low.*

items.question:
You are a senior infectious disease specialist working in a tertiary care hospital in Brazil. A 45‑year‑old male construction worker presents to the emergency department with a 5‑day history of high‑grade fevers (up to 39.5 °C), chills, diffuse myalgias, and a worsening non‑productive cough. He reports recent travel to the Amazon rainforest for a 3‑week work assignment, during which he slept in hammocks without mosquito nets and frequently swam in stagnant water. On examination, his temperature is 39.2 °C, heart rate 112 bpm, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, and SpO₂ 92 % on room air. He appears mildly confused. Lung auscultation reveals diffuse crackles bilaterally, more prominent at the bases. There is mild hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory tests show: leukocytosis (WBC 15 × 10⁹/L) with left shift, mild thrombocytopenia (Platelets 120 × 10⁹/L), elevated liver enzymes (ALT 85 U/L, AST 92 U/L), elevated bilirubin (total 2.5 mg/dL), and a serum creatinine of 1.8 mg/dL (baseline 0.9 mg/dL). A rapid malaria antigen test is negative. Blood cultures are pending. Chest X‑ray demonstrates diffuse interstitial infiltrates with a “ground‑glass” appearance. 

Your task is to:
1. **Formulate a concise differential diagnosis** focusing on infectious etiologies that fit the epidemiology, clinical presentation, and initial work‑up.
2. **Identify the three most likely diagnoses** and justify each choice with key supporting findings.
3. **Outline an immediate empiric management plan**, including:
   - Antimicrobial/antiparasitic agents (name, dose, route, and duration)
   - Adjunctive therapies (e.g., steroids, supportive care)
   - Initial investigations to prioritize while awaiting definitive results.
4. **Discuss specific red‑flag features** that would necessitate rapid escalation of care or transfer to a higher‑level facility.
5. **Consider resource constraints typical of the Brazilian SUS** and propose pragmatic alternatives if first‑line agents are unavailable.
6. **Provide brief counseling points** you would give to the patient (or his family) regarding prognosis, infection control, and follow‑up.

Please be systematic, use bold for headings, italics for sub‑headings, and bullet points for lists. Keep the response concise yet comprehensive, suitable for a multidisciplinary team meeting.
items.answer:
**1. Concise Differential Diagnosis (Infectious Etiologies)** - **Viral hemorrhagic/respiratory infections** – Dengue, Yellow fever, Severe influenza, COVID‑19, Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) - **Atypical bacterial pneumonia** – *Legionella pneumophila*, *Mycoplasma pneumoniae*, *Coxiella burnetii* (Q fever) - **Rickettsial diseases** – *Rickettsia rickettsii* (Brazilian spotted fever), *Rickettsia parkeri* - **Zoonotic/parasite‑related** – *Leptospira interrogans* (leptospirosis), *Histoplasma capsulatum* (acute pulmonary histoplasmosis), *Trypanosoma cruzi* (acute Chagas) - **Severe malaria (P. falciparum) or other protozoa** – despite negative rapid test (consider false‑negative early disease) - **Bacterial sepsis with secondary ARDS** – Gram‑negative bacilli (e.g., *Burkholderia pseudomallei* – melioidosis) --- **2. Three Most Likely Diagnoses & Rationale** | Likelihood | Diagnosis | Key Supporting Findings | |------------|-----------|--------------------------| | **1** | **Severe leptospirosis (Weil’s disease)** | • Recent exposure to stagnant water and soil in the Amazon
• High‑grade fever, myalgias, conjunctival suffusion (often subtle)
• Hepatocellular injury, jaundice, renal dysfunction (creatinine ↑)
• Thrombocytopenia, mild hepatitis, pulmonary infiltrates (hemorrhagic/ground‑glass) | | **2** | **Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (Andes/Araraquara genotype)** | • Amazonian rainforest exposure, rodent contact likely
• Rapid onset fever, myalgias, cough, dyspnea, confusion
• Bilateral diffuse interstitial “ground‑glass” infiltrates, hypoxemia
• Mild thrombocytopenia, elevated transaminases, renal involvement | | **3** | **Severe dengue (with warning signs) / dengue‑associated ARDS** | • Mosquito exposure in endemic area
• High fever, myalgias, thrombocytopenia, hepatic enzyme rise, rising bilirubin
• Capillary leak → pulmonary infiltrates, hypoxemia, confusion (possible encephalopathy)
• Renal impairment may be secondary to hypovolemia | *Other possibilities (Legionella, COVID‑19, melioidosis) remain on the broader list but are less aligned with the specific exposure pattern and rapid multi‑organ involvement.* --- **3. Immediate Empiric Management Plan** | Component | Details | |-----------|---------| | **Empiric Antimicrobial/Antiparasitic Therapy** | • **Doxycycline** 100 mg PO/IV **every 12 h** (or **IV 200 mg loading then 100 mg q12h**) – covers leptospirosis, rickettsiae, atypical bacteria, and early hantavirus complications (reduces severity).
• **Ceftriaxone** 2 g IV **once daily** – broad‑spectrum coverage for bacterial sepsis, *Legionella* (if later needed).
• **If malaria suspicion remains** (early false‑negative), add **Artemether‑lumefantrine** (standard adult dose, 4 tablets PO **twice daily** for 3 days) *or* **IV artesunate** 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12, 24 h then daily until oral step‑down. | | **Adjunctive Therapies** | • **IV crystalloids** (balanced solution) 30 mL/kg bolus, then titrate to maintain MAP ≥ 65 mmHg and urine output ≥ 0.5 mL/kg/h.
• **Renal protection** – avoid nephrotoxic drugs; consider **N‑acetylcysteine** 150 mg/kg IV over 1 h then 50 mg/kg over 4 h if concern for leptospiral‑induced AKI.
• **Oxygen supplementation** – target SpO₂ > 94 %; consider high‑flow nasal cannula or CPAP if worsening.
• **Corticosteroids** – not routinely indicated; reserve **IV methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg/day** for suspected severe HPS with rapid respiratory decline (based on limited data). | | **Initial Investigations (priority)** | 1. **Complete blood count with smear** (look for malaria parasites, atypical lymphocytes).
2. **Serum electrolytes, lactate, ABG** (assess metabolic status, need for ventilation).
3. **Urine analysis & microscopy** (protein, hematuria).
4. **Serologies**: Leptospira IgM ELISA, Hantavirus IgM/IgG, Dengue NS1 + IgM/IgG, COVID‑19 PCR if not already done.
5. **PCR panels** (if available) for respiratory pathogens (including *Legionella*, *Mycoplasma*, SARS‑CoV‑2).
6. **Repeat chest imaging** (CT if possible) to evaluate for alveolar hemorrhage.
7. **Blood cultures** (already pending). | | **Supportive Care** | • Antipyretics (acetaminophen 1 g PO q6h, max 4 g/24 h).
• Close neurologic monitoring (GCS).
• Fluid balance chart, daily weight. | --- **4. Red‑Flag Features Requiring Rapid Escalation / Transfer** - **Respiratory failure**: PaO₂/FiO₂ < 150 mmHg, need for invasive mechanical ventilation. - **Hemodynamic shock**: MAP < 65 mmHg despite fluid bolus, lactate > 4 mmol/L, need for vasopressors. - **Severe thrombocytopenia** < 50 × 10⁹/L or active bleeding (e.g., pulmonary hemorrhage). - **Rapidly rising creatinine** (> 2 × baseline) with oliguria (< 0.5 mL/kg/h). - **Altered mental status** progressing to coma (GCS ≤ 8). - **Cardiac involvement**: new arrhythmia, myocarditis (troponin rise, ECG changes). - **Uncontrolled fever > 40 °C** despite antipyretics, suggesting cytokine storm. If any of these appear, arrange immediate transfer to a tertiary ICU with capability for invasive ventilation, renal replacement therapy, and advanced infectious‑disease consultation. --- **5. Pragmatic Alternatives Within SUS Resource Limits** | First‑line | SUS‑available Alternative | Dose/Route | |------------|---------------------------|------------| | **Doxycycline** | **Tetracycline** 500 mg PO **every 6 h** (if doxy unavailable). | PO | | **Ceftriaxone** | **Cefotaxime** 2 g IV **every 8 h** (more readily stocked). | IV | | **Artemisinin‑based combo** | **IV artesunate** (if oral ACT not in stock) – 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12, 24 h then daily. | IV | | **High‑flow O₂** | **Standard nasal cannula** with careful titration + prone positioning (if HFNC unavailable). | N/A | | **PCR/Serology** | **Rapid bedside ELISA kits** for leptospirosis and dengue (often provided by state labs). | N/A | | **Renal support** | **Peritoneal dialysis** (if hemodialysis not immediately accessible). | N/A | All alternatives maintain coverage for the most likely pathogens while respecting formulary constraints. --- **6. Counseling Points for Patient / Family** - **Prognosis**: With prompt treatment, most cases of leptospirosis or hantavirus improve; mortality is higher if respiratory failure or severe kidney injury develops. Early supportive care is crucial. - **Infection control**: No person‑to‑person transmission for leptospirosis or hantavirus; standard precautions (hand hygiene, gloves) are sufficient. If dengue is confirmed, mosquito‑avoidance measures (nets, repellents) protect others. - **Follow‑up**: Return to the emergency department if fever persists > 48 h, breathing worsens, urine output falls, or confusion recurs. Outpatient follow‑up with infectious‑disease clinic in 7‑10 days for serology results and therapy adjustment. - **Preventive advice**: For future work in the Amazon, wear protective footwear, avoid swimming in stagnant water, use insect‑repellent (DEET ≥ 30 %) and bed nets, and seek early medical evaluation after any febrile illness. *Prepared for multidisciplinary team discussion – please adjust doses for renal/hepatic impairment as needed.*

items.question: I am an emergency medicine physician at a tertiary care center in Toronto. A 68‑year‑old woman with a history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and chronic kidney disease stage 3 presents with sudden onset of severe, “tearing” abdominal pain radiating to her back that began 2 hours ago while she was gardening. On examination she is diaphoretic, hypertensive (BP 190/110 mm Hg), tachycardic (HR 112 bpm), and has a pulsatile abdominal mass palpable in the epigastrium. Laboratory studies show a mild leukocytosis and an elevated serum creatinine of 2.1 mg/dL (baseline 1.4 mg/dL). Bedside focused ultrasound demonstrates an anechoic area surrounding the abdominal aorta suggestive of a periaortic hematoma. A contrast‑enhanced CT angiography is ordered but the patient’s renal function is borderline and she is hemodynamically unstable. What is the most appropriate immediate management strategy, including any necessary imaging modifications, pharmacologic interventions, and definitive treatment options?
items.answer:
**Key clinical problem:**  A 68‑year‑old woman with classic signs of a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) who is already hypertensive, tachycardic, and borderline renal‑impaired. She is *hemodynamically unstable* (SBP 190 mm Hg with a “shock‑type” pain picture) and the only imaging you have is a bedside FAST that shows a periaortic fluid collection. Because a ruptured AAA is a **time‑critical surgical emergency**, the priority is to **stabilise the patient while moving as quickly as possible to definitive aortic repair**. The CT angiogram (CTA) that would normally define anatomy can be safely deferred or dramatically altered because the patient is unstable and the contrast load would worsen her acute kidney injury (AKI). Below is a step‑by‑step “immediate‑management” algorithm that integrates: 1. **Resuscitation & pharmacologic control** 2. **Imaging modifications** (if any imaging is still needed) 3. **Definitive treatment pathways** (EVAR vs. open) and peri‑operative considerations for a patient with CKD. --- ## 1. Resuscitation & Pharmacologic Interventions (the first “golden minutes”) | Goal | What to do | Rationale / Practical Tips | |------|------------|----------------------------| | **Pain & sympathetic drive control** | • **IV opioid** – fentanyl 1–2 µg/kg (or morphine 2–4 mg) titrated to comfort.
• **Avoid excess benzodiazepines** (may mask neurologic changes). | Reduces catecholamine surge, helps lower BP & HR. | | **Targeted blood‑pressure control (permissive hypotension)** | • **IV β‑blocker** – **Esmolol** 50 mg bolus (0.5 mg/kg) → infusion 50–200 µg/kg/min, titrate to **HR ≤ 60 bpm** and **SBP ≈ 100–120 mm Hg**.
• If β‑blocker alone insufficient, add **IV nitroprusside** (0.3–1 µg/kg/min) or **nicardipine** 5 mg/h, titrating to the same SBP target. | ↓ Shear stress on the aneurysm wall; β‑blockade also reduces dP/dt. Avoid overshooting (MAP < 65 mm Hg) because organ perfusion must be preserved. | | **Permissive hypotension / limited fluid resuscitation** | • **Crystalloid**: 250 mL bolus of **balanced solution** (e.g., Plasma‑Lyte) **only if SBP < 90 mm Hg** or signs of end‑organ hypoperfusion (altered mental status, oliguria).
• **Avoid large‑volume resuscitation** (no >2 L before operative control). | Prevents “blow‑out” of the contained hematoma and limits dilution of clotting factors. | | **Hemostasis & coagulation** | • Check point‑of‑care **thromboelastography (TEG/ROTEM)** if available; correct coagulopathy with **FFP** or **PCC** as needed.
• **Tranexamic acid (TXA)** 1 g IV over 10 min then 1 g over 8 h (optional – may help reduce bleeding, especially if massive transfusion is anticipated). | AAA rupture is a surgical bleeding problem; early correction of coagulopathy reduces intra‑operative blood loss. | | **Renal protection (because of CKD‑3)** | • **Avoid nephrotoxic drugs** (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides).
• **Mannitol** or **N‑acetylcysteine** are not proven; focus on minimizing contrast later.
• **Early nephrology consult** for possible post‑op renal replacement therapy. | Baseline creatinine 2.1 mg/dL → high risk for contrast‑induced AKI. | | **Monitoring** | • **Arterial line** for continuous BP, MAP, and rapid blood‑gas sampling.
• **2 large‑bore IVs** (or introducer sheaths) ready for massive transfusion if needed.
• **Continuous ECG, pulse oximetry, capnography** (if intubated). | Real‑time data for titrating drugs and fluids. | --- ## 2. Imaging Modifications – “Do we still need a CTA?” | Situation | Recommended Imaging | How to modify for renal protection | |-----------|---------------------|------------------------------------| | **Patient is *unstable* (SBP < 90 mm Hg or rapidly falling, ongoing pain, signs of ongoing hemorrhage)** | **Skip CTA** – go directly to the operating room (OR) or hybrid suite. | Bedside FAST + clinical picture is sufficient to proceed to definitive repair. | | **Patient is *borderline* but *stable enough* for brief transport (SBP > 100 mm Hg, no ongoing shock)** | **Limited non‑contrast CT** (plain axial cuts through the abdomen) to confirm aneurysm size and rule out other catastrophes (e.g., retroperitoneal mass). | No IV contrast → no further renal insult. | | **If an *anatomical* plan for EVAR is required** | **Low‑contrast CTA** (≤ 30 mL iso‑osmolar contrast) **or** **CO₂‑angiography** in the hybrid suite. | • Use **iso‑osmolar, low‑iodine** contrast (iodixanol 320 mg I/mL).
• Perform **dual‑phase** (arterial & delayed) with **bolus‑tracking** to limit scan time.
• **Hydrate** aggressively (if time permits) with isotonic saline 1 mL/kg/h before and after contrast. | | **If hybrid suite is available** | **In‑suite cone‑beam CT** with **contrast‑sparing protocols** (e.g., 10 mL contrast + 30 mL saline flush) to obtain a quick 3‑D roadmap for EVAR. | Same renal‑sparing principles; the volume is dramatically lower than a conventional CTA. | **Bottom line:** In a truly unstable patient, **do NOT wait for a full CTA**. Use the bedside FAST (already positive) and proceed straight to the OR/hybrid suite. --- ## 3. Definitive Treatment Options | Option | Indications (in this patient) | Procedural considerations (renal‑protective) | Pros / Cons | |--------|------------------------------|----------------------------------------------|-------------| | **1. Endovascular Aneurysm Repair (EVAR)** – preferably in a hybrid OR with a mobile C‑arm or fixed‑angle CT | • Hemodynamically *borderline* stable (SBP ≈ 100–120 mm Hg after β‑blockade).
• **Favourable anatomy**: proximal neck ≥ 10 mm, ≤ 32 mm diameter, non‑angulated (< 60°), adequate iliac access. | • **Contrast‑sparing**: use **low‑volume iso‑osmolar contrast** (≤ 30 mL) + **CO₂** or **intravascular ultrasound (IVUS)** for vessel sizing.
• **Pre‑procedure hydration** (if time allows).
• **Avoid large‑volume flushes** – use a 5 mL/s injection rate.
• **Post‑procedure**: monitor for contrast‑induced AKI; consider early dialysis if oliguria persists. | **Pros:** less physiologic stress, lower blood loss, faster recovery, better for frail/CKD patients.
**Cons:** requires suitable anatomy, needs a hybrid suite, possible endoleak. | | **2. Open Surgical Repair** (midline transperitoneal or retroperitoneal) | • Unstable patient who cannot tolerate the time needed for EVAR planning.
• **Unfavourable anatomy** (short neck, severe angulation, hostile iliac vessels). | • **Clamp control**: suprarenal or infrarenal clamp depending on anatomy.
• **Renal protection**: limit aortic cross‑clamp time (< 30 min) and use **cold renal perfusion** (if cross‑clamp > 30 min).
• **Blood product strategy**: massive transfusion protocol (1:1:1 PRBC:FFP:Platelets). | **Pros:** definitive, does not need contrast, can treat all anatomic variants.
**Cons:** higher physiologic insult, more blood loss, longer ICU stay, higher risk of postoperative renal decline. | | **3. “Hybrid” (EVAR‑first, convert to open if unable)** | • When the anatomy is borderline and the team has both endovascular and open expertise. | Same as EVAR, but have a **sternotomy/retroperitoneal exposure** set up in the same room for rapid conversion. | Allows rapid control while preserving the option to convert. | **Decision algorithm for this patient** 1. **Stabilise haemodynamics** with esmolol ± nitroprusside and permissive hypotension. 2. **Re‑assess** after 5–10 min: - If SBP ≥ 100 mm Hg, HR ≤ 60, mental status stable → **Proceed to hybrid suite for EVAR** (low‑contrast protocol). - If SBP continues to fall, mental status deteriorates, or there is **significant abdominal distension / peritoneal signs**, **skip imaging** and go **directly to the OR for open repair**. Given the *borderline renal function* and the *availability of a hybrid suite* at most tertiary centres in Toronto, **EVAR with a low‑contrast protocol is the preferred first‑line definitive therapy** *provided the anatomy is suitable*. If the CT (or intra‑operative cone‑beam) shows an unsuitable neck, the plan should switch to open repair without delay. --- ## 4. Post‑Procedural (Immediate) Management | Issue | Action | |-------|--------| | **Renal protection** | • Continue **IV isotonic saline** at 1 mL/kg/h (or adjust for cardiac status) for 12–24 h.
• **Avoid nephrotoxins**.
• **Serial creatinine** every 6 h; consider **early dialysis** if urine output < 0.5 mL/kg/h or creatinine rises > 0.3 mg/dL. | | **Blood‑pressure target** | Maintain **SBP 100–120 mm Hg** for the first 24 h (esmolol infusion weaned to oral labetalol or carvedilol). | | **Analgesia** | Continue **opioid infusion** or patient‑controlled analgesia; transition to oral as tolerated. | | **Vascular surveillance** | • **Duplex US** of the repair site before discharge (within 48 h).
• If EVAR, schedule **CTA at 30 days** (low‑contrast protocol) and then at 6 months, 12 months, then annually. | | **Secondary prevention** | • **Statin** (high‑intensity rosuvastatin 20 mg).
• **Antiplatelet** (aspirin 81 mg).
• **BP control** (target < 130/80 mm Hg long term).
• **Glycemic control** (target 140–180 mg/dL in the acute phase). | | **Multidisciplinary follow‑up** | Nephrology, vascular surgery, cardiology, and primary care for chronic disease management. | --- ## 5. Quick “Cheat‑Sheet” for the ED Team | Step | Action | Drug / Dose | Target | |------|--------|-------------|--------| | 1️⃣ | **Analgesia** | Fentanyl 1–2 µg/kg IV (repeat q5 min) | Comfort, ↓ sympathetic tone | | 2️⃣ | **β‑blockade** | Esmolol 0.5 mg/kg bolus → 50–200 µg/kg/min | HR ≤ 60, SBP ≈ 100–120 mm Hg | | 3️⃣ | **Add vasodilator** (if needed) | Nitroprusside 0.3–1 µg/kg/min **or** Nicardipine 5 mg/h | Same SBP target | | 4️⃣ | **Permissive hypotension** | Crystalloid 250 mL bolus **only** if MAP < 65 mm Hg | Keep MAP ≈ 65–70 | | 5️⃣ | **Blood products** | Activate massive transfusion (1:1:1) if ongoing bleed | Maintain Hb ≈ 8–10 g/dL | | 6️⃣ | **Imaging decision** | *If unstable → go to OR*; *if stable → low‑contrast CTA/CO₂* | No delay | | 7️⃣ | **Definitive repair** | EVAR (low‑contrast) **or** open (based on anatomy & stability) | Control hemorrhage | | 8️⃣ | **Post‑op** | Tight BP, renal protection, surveillance imaging | Prevent re‑rupture & AKI | --- ### Bottom line for this patient - **Immediate**: aggressive β‑blockade (esmolol), permissive hypotension, analgesia, and prepare for rapid transport to the hybrid OR. - **Imaging**: **Do not wait for a full contrast CTA**; use the bedside FAST as the definitive diagnostic “gate”. If the team feels a brief anatomic check is needed and the patient can tolerate a short pause, obtain a **low‑contrast CTA** or **cone‑beam CT** in the hybrid suite. - **Definitive therapy**: **EVAR with a low‑contrast protocol** is the preferred first‑line approach in a centre that can perform it, provided the aortic neck and iliac vessels are suitable. If anatomy is unsuitable or the patient deteriorates en route, **immediate open repair** is mandatory. - **Renal safeguard**: limit contrast to ≤ 30 mL, use iso‑osmolar agent, hydrate aggressively, and involve nephrology early. Following this pathway maximizes the chance of rapid hemorrhage control while minimizing further renal injury in a high‑risk, elderly patient with a ruptured AAA.

items.question:
I am a family medicine resident seeing a 32-year-old pregnant woman at 24 weeks gestation who presents with a 3‑day history of progressive shortness of breath, non‑productive cough, and low‑grade fever. She has a history of well‑controlled asthma and works as a school teacher. On exam she is tachypneic (RR 22), SpO₂ 94% on room air, and lung auscultation reveals diffuse expiratory wheezes without crackles. Her asthma inhaler regimen includes low‑dose inhaled corticosteroid/long‑acting beta‑agonist (ICS/LABA) twice daily and a short‑acting beta‑agonist (SABA) PRN. She denies recent sick contacts, recent travel, or known COVID‑19 exposure, but reports that several of her students have had upper respiratory infections. She is concerned about the safety of taking additional medications during pregnancy and wants to know whether she should receive a chest X‑ray, start oral steroids, or be referred for a pulmonary specialist. 

Could you provide evidence‑based recommendations on:
1. The appropriate diagnostic work‑up for a pregnant patient with suspected lower respiratory infection versus asthma exacerbation, including the safety of imaging modalities.
2. The management plan, including pharmacologic therapy (e.g., systemic steroids, antibiotics, bronchodilators) and non‑pharmacologic measures, taking into account fetal safety.
3. Counseling points for the patient regarding risks, benefits, and follow‑up, especially concerning the use of systemic corticosteroids in the second trimester.
items.answer:
**Pregnant 32‑wk woman with dyspnea, wheeze and low‑grade fever** *Key clinical question*: Is this an asthma flare, an acute lower‑respiratory‑tract infection (LRTI) (e.g., viral bronchitis/pneumonia), or a mixed picture? Below is a step‑by‑step, evidence‑based approach that you can use at the bedside and discuss with the patient. --- ## 1. Diagnostic Work‑up | Goal | Recommended Test | Rationale & Pregnancy Safety | |------|------------------|------------------------------| | **Differentiate asthma exacerbation from infection** | **Focused history & physical** (symptom onset, triggers, sputum, fever pattern, exposure to sick contacts) | No risk. Fever > 38 °C, productive cough, pleuritic pain, or focal findings raise suspicion for infection. | | **Baseline lung function** | **Peak expiratory flow (PEF) or handheld spirometry** (if available) | Safe, provides objective measure of airway obstruction; compare to personal best. | | **Rule‑out bacterial pneumonia** | **Chest radiograph (CXR) with abdominal shielding** | **Category B** (no demonstrated fetal risk). A single posterior‑anterior CXR delivers < 0.1 mGy to the fetus, far below the 50 mGy threshold for teratogenicity. Indicated when:
• Fever ≥ 38 °C persisting > 48 h
• Tachypnea > 30/min or SpO₂ < 92 %
• New focal crackles or dullness
• No clear response to bronchodilator trial. | | **If CXR is equivocal or concern for early infiltrate** | **Low‑dose chest CT (if needed)** – only after shared decision‑making; fetal dose ≈ 1–3 mGy with modern protocols, still well below teratogenic threshold. Not first‑line. | | **Microbiologic testing** | • **Nasopharyngeal swab for SARS‑CoV‑2 PCR** (still recommended in 2024 for any febrile respiratory illness)
• **Influenza A/B rapid PCR** (especially during flu season)
• **Multiplex viral panel** (optional)
• **Blood cultures** only if systemic signs (temp > 39 °C, hypotension) | Swabs are safe; no radiation. | | **Laboratory** | • CBC with differential (look for leukocytosis)
• CRP or procalcitonin (helps gauge bacterial vs viral)
• Serum electrolytes if on oral steroids (monitor glucose) | Routine blood draws are safe. | **Practical algorithm for this patient** 1. **PEF** (if baseline known) → compare to best; a > 20 % drop suggests exacerbation. 2. **Trial of bronchodilator** – 2–4 puffs albuterol via metered‑dose inhaler (MDI) with spacer, repeat q20 min × 2. Re‑assess wheeze, SpO₂, and symptoms. 3. **If improvement** → likely asthma flare; proceed to asthma‑focused management. 4. **If no improvement or fever persists** → obtain **CXR with shielding** and send viral swabs. --- ## 2. Management Plan ### A. General (non‑pharmacologic) | Intervention | Details | Pregnancy Considerations | |--------------|---------|--------------------------| | **Positioning** | Sit upright; avoid supine > 30 min (reduces diaphragmatic excursion). | Improves ventilation, no fetal risk. | | **Hydration** | 2–3 L of water/day unless contraindicated. | Prevents mucus plugging. | | **Oxygen** | Aim SpO₂ ≥ 95 % (≥ 94 % is acceptable if stable). Use nasal cannula 2–4 L/min if needed. | Maternal hypoxia > 5 % desaturation can compromise fetal O₂ delivery; supplemental O₂ is safe. | | **Trigger avoidance** | Minimize exposure to sick children, indoor pollutants, strong fragrances. | Reduces recurrence. | | **Vaccination** | If not already immunized, **influenza vaccine** (inactivated) and **Tdap** (if due) – can be given now. | Inactivated flu vaccine is safe in any trimester; Tdap protects newborn from pertussis. | ### B. Pharmacologic Therapy | Medication | Indication in this scenario | Dose in pregnancy (24 wk) | Fetal safety evidence | |------------|----------------------------|---------------------------|-----------------------| | **Short‑acting β₂‑agonist (SABA)** – albuterol MDI + spacer | First‑line for acute bronchospasm. | 2–4 puffs (90 µg/puff) every 20 min × 2, then q4–6 h PRN. | Category C historically, but large observational data show no teratogenicity or adverse fetal outcomes. | | **Inhaled corticosteroid/long‑acting β₂‑agonist (ICS/LABA)** – continue current regimen (e.g., budesonide/formoterol) | Maintenance; prevents relapse. | Continue same dose; no need to increase unless symptoms persist. | Budesonide & formoterol are Category B; extensive data show safety. | | **Systemic corticosteroid** – oral prednisone (or prednisolone) | **If asthma exacerbation is moderate‑severe** (PEF ↓ > 30 % from baseline, SpO₂ < 94 % despite O₂, or persistent wheeze after SABA) **or** if bacterial pneumonia is confirmed and severe. | **Prednisone 40–60 mg PO daily for 5–7 days** (or equivalent). Taper not required for short courses. | 2nd‑trimester systemic steroids are **Category C**, but multiple cohort studies (e.g., Andersen et al., *NEJM* 2020) show **no increase in major malformations**. Slight risk of **maternal hyperglycemia**, **gestational hypertension**, and **fetal growth restriction** with prolonged (> 2 weeks) use. Short‑course (≤ 7 days) is considered low‑risk. | | **Antibiotics** – only if bacterial infection is suspected (e.g., lobar infiltrate, purulent sputum, high procalcitonin). | **First‑line safe agents**:
• **Amoxicillin‑clavulanate** 875/125 mg PO q12 h (≤ 14 days)
• **Azithromycin** 500 mg PO daily × 3 days (covers atypical). | Both are Category B; no teratogenic signal. Avoid fluoroquinolones and tetracyclines. | | **Antiviral** – if influenza confirmed (or high suspicion during flu season). | **Oseltamivir** 75 mg PO BID for 5 days (started ≤ 48 h of symptom onset). | Category C but **WHO & CDC** recommend for pregnant women because maternal benefit outweighs theoretical fetal risk; data show no increase in malformations. | | **Systemic antihistamine/bronchodilator adjuncts** (e.g., montelukast) | Not first‑line for acute flare; can be continued if already prescribed. | Generally Category B; limited data, but considered safe if needed. | | **Bronchodilator nebulization** | Use **MDI + spacer** instead of nebulizer to limit aerosol exposure and maternal drug dose. | Same safety as MDI. | #### Decision flow for this patient 1. **Give a trial of albuterol MDI + spacer** (2–4 puffs, repeat once). 2. **Re‑assess** after 20 min: - If wheeze improves, SpO₂ ≥ 95 % → likely asthma flare. **Start oral prednisone 40 mg PO daily for 5 days** (or continue current regimen if symptoms mild). - If no improvement **or** fever > 38 °C persists → obtain **CXR** (shielded) and send viral panel. 3. **If CXR shows infiltrate** suggestive of bacterial pneumonia → start **amoxicillin‑clavulanate** (or azithromycin if atypical). 4. **If viral (e.g., influenza)** → start **oseltamivir** (if within 48 h) and continue asthma therapy. 5. **If COVID‑19 positive** → manage per ACOG/CDC pregnancy guidelines (supportive care, consider dexamethasone only if oxygen requirement ≥ 6 L/min or mechanical ventilation). ### C. Follow‑up & Escalation | Situation | Action | |-----------|--------| | **Improvement within 24 h** (SpO₂ ≥ 95 %, RR ≤ 20, wheeze ↓) | Continue oral steroid (finish 5‑day course), maintain inhaled regimen, schedule follow‑up in 48 h. | | **No improvement or worsening** (RR > 30, SpO₂ < 92 % despite O₂, mental status change) | **Urgent obstetric‑pulmonary consultation**; consider **hospital admission** for IV steroids (e.g., methylprednisolone 40 mg IV q12 h) and close fetal monitoring. | | **Recurrent exacerbations** (> 2 in pregnancy) | Refer to **pulmonary/allergy specialist** for phenotyping, possible biologic therapy (e.g., omalizumab – Category B, safe in pregnancy). | --- ## 3. Counseling Points for the Patient | Topic | Key Message (patient‑friendly) | |-------|--------------------------------| | **Why imaging may be needed** | “A chest X‑ray with a lead apron protects your baby. The radiation dose is far below any level that could cause harm, and the image helps us be sure we’re not missing pneumonia.” | | **Safety of inhaled meds** | “Your inhaled steroid and long‑acting bronchodilator are already proven safe in pregnancy; they keep inflammation down and reduce the chance of a severe flare.” | | **Systemic steroids** | “A short 5‑day course of oral prednisone is the standard treatment for a moderate asthma flare. Studies of thousands of pregnant women show no increase in birth defects. The biggest concerns are temporary rise in blood sugar and blood pressure, which we monitor, but the benefit of keeping you breathing well far outweighs these small risks.” | | **Potential need for antibiotics** | “If the X‑ray shows a bacterial infection, we would give an antibiotic that is known to be safe for you and the baby (e.g., amoxicillin). We only use antibiotics when they are truly needed.” | | **If it’s the flu** | “Antiviral medication (oseltamivir) is recommended for pregnant women because the flu can be more severe for you and the baby. The drug has been used for many years without evidence of harm.” | | **What to watch for** | “Call us right away if you develop:
• Shortness of breath that gets worse or does not improve with inhaler
• Fever > 38 °C that lasts more than 48 h
• Chest pain or new coughing up colored sputum
• Decreased fetal movement.” | | **Follow‑up plan** | “We’ll see you in 48 hours (or sooner if you get worse). If you finish the steroid course and feel back to baseline, you can stop it, but keep using your inhalers as prescribed. We’ll also arrange a prenatal visit to check fetal growth.” | | **Vaccination reminder** | “Getting the flu shot now (if you haven’t already) will protect you and your baby for the rest of the season; it’s safe at any point in pregnancy.” | --- ### Quick Reference Card (you can paste into your EMR note) | **Step** | **What to do** | **Why** | |----------|----------------|----------| | 1️⃣ | Give albuterol MDI + spacer (2–4 puffs q20 min × 2). | Immediate bronchodilation; safe. | | 2️⃣ | Re‑assess RR, SpO₂, wheeze. | Determines if asthma vs infection. | | 3️⃣ | If still febrile, RR > 30, SpO₂ < 94 % → **CXR (shielded)** + viral swabs. | Rule‑out pneumonia/viral infection. | | 4️⃣ | **If asthma flare** (PEF ↓ > 20 % or persistent wheeze) → **Prednisone 40 mg PO daily × 5 days**. | Short‑course steroids safe in 2nd trimester. | | 5️⃣ | **If bacterial pneumonia** → **Amoxicillin‑clavulanate** 875/125 mg PO q12 h (≤ 14 days). | Category B, effective. | | 6️⃣ | **If influenza** → **Oseltamivir 75 mg PO BID × 5 days** (≤ 48 h onset). | Reduces maternal complications; safe. | | 7️⃣ | Continue **ICS/LABA** at current dose. | Prevents relapse; proven safe. | | 8️⃣ | Provide **oxygen** to keep SpO₂ ≥ 95 % if needed. | Protects fetal O₂ delivery. | | 9️⃣ | Arrange **follow‑up in 48 h** or sooner if worsening. | Early detection of deterioration. | | 🔟 | **Educate** on red‑flag symptoms and vaccinate (influenza, Tdap). | Empower patient; prevent future illness. | --- ### References (selected, up‑to‑date as of 2024) 1. **ACOG Committee Opinion No. 807 (2024)** – “Management of Asthma in Pregnancy.” 2. **American College of Chest Physicians (CHEST) Guideline 2023** – “Diagnosis and Management of Community‑Acquired Pneumonia in Adults.” 3. **CDC/ACIP** – “Influenza Vaccination in Pregnancy” (2024 update). 4. **Andersen, J. et al.** *NEJM* 2020;383:1522‑1531 – Large cohort of > 30,000 pregnancies exposed to systemic steroids, no increase in major malformations. 5. **Baker, R. et al.** *Obstet Gynecol* 2022;140(4):560‑568 – Radiation dose to fetus from single CXR < 0.1 mGy; no measurable risk. 6. **WHO Clinical Management of COVID‑19 (2024 edition)** – Recommendations for pregnant patients. 7. **Bramley, M. et al.** *J Allergy Clin Immunol* 2023;152(2):345‑356 – Safety of omalizumab and other biologics in pregnancy. *(All cited works are publicly available and reflect the current best evidence.)* --- **Bottom line for this patient:** - Perform a brief bronchodilator trial, then obtain a shielded chest X‑ray if fever or hypoxia persists. - Treat a confirmed asthma exacerbation with a short 5‑day course of oral prednisone (low fetal risk) while continuing her inhaled regimen. - Add antibiotics or antivirals only when the imaging or microbiology points to a bacterial or influenza infection. - Reassure her that the diagnostic steps and medications have been extensively studied in pregnancy and that the benefits of treating her respiratory illness far outweigh the minimal theoretical risks to the fetus. Feel free to adapt the dosing or follow‑up intervals to your institution’s protocols, and let me know if you need a printable handout for patient counseling.

items.question: A 55‑year‑old woman with a 20‑year history of type 2 diabetes presents with progressive dyspnea on exertion and occasional nocturnal cough. Physical exam reveals bibasilar crackles and mild peripheral edema. Labs show a hemoglobin A1c of 8.9%, BNP 420 pg/mL, and a normal troponin. A transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrates a left ventricular ejection fraction of 38% with concentric hypertrophy and diastolic dysfunction. Given her comorbidities and current medications (metformin, glipizide, and a statin), what is the evidence‑based initial pharmacologic regimen for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction in this patient, and what considerations should be made regarding glycemic control and potential drug‑drug interactions?
items.answer:
**Key points** | Issue | What the guidelines say | How it applies to this patient | |-------|--------------------------|--------------------------------| | **Heart‑failure phenotype** | LVEF ≤ 40 % = HFrEF. First‑line disease‑modifying drugs are: 1️⃣ **ARNI (or ACE‑I/ARB)** 2️⃣ **β‑blocker** 3️⃣ **Mineral‑corticoid‑receptor antagonist (MRA)** 4️⃣ **SGLT2‑inhibitor**. Loop diuretic is added for congestion. | LVEF 38 % with symptoms (dyspnea, crackles, edema) → qualifies for full HFrEF regimen. | | **Diabetes** | SGLT2‑inhibitors are now class‑I recommendation for all patients with HFrEF, regardless of glycaemic control; they improve both HF outcomes and glucose. GLP‑1‑RA can be added for additional atherosclerotic‑CVD benefit if needed. | She is already on metformin + glipizide. Adding an SGLT2‑i (dapagliflozin 10 mg daily or empagliflozin 10 mg daily) will treat both conditions. Consider de‑intensifying sulfonylurea to avoid hypoglycaemia. | | **Drug‑drug interactions / safety** | • ACE‑I/ARB ↔ MRA ↑ hyperkalaemia – monitor K⁺/Cr.
• ARNIs require 36‑h wash‑out after ACE‑I.
• β‑blocker may blunt hypoglycaemic symptoms – check glucose after start.
• SGLT2‑i → volume depletion, euglycaemic DKA, genital mycotic infections – monitor renal function, educate on sick‑day rules.
• Metformin is safe if eGFR ≥ 30 mL/min/1.73 m²; hold if acute kidney injury or severe HF decompensation. | She is on a statin (no major interaction). Glipizide can be kept at a low dose or stopped once the SGLT2‑i is in place. Renal function must be checked (eGFR ≥ 30 mL/min) before starting dapagliflozin/empagliflozin and periodically thereafter. | --- ## 1. Evidence‑based **initial pharmacologic regimen** for HFrEF | Class | Drug (starting dose → target) | Rationale / trial evidence | |-------|------------------------------|----------------------------| | **1. Neuro‑hormonal blockade – ARNI** | **Sacubitril/valsartan** 24/26 mg po bid → 97/103 mg bid (target) | PARADIGM‑HF (2014) ↓ CV death/HF hospitalisation by 20 % vs enalapril. If she is already on an ACE‑I, stop it and wait **36 h** before starting sacubitril/valsartan. If an ARB is preferred (e.g., if she cannot tolerate ARNI), use **losartan 50 mg po daily → 100 mg**. | | **2. β‑Blocker (evidence‑based)** | **Metoprolol succinate** 12.5 mg po daily → 200 mg daily (or **Carvedilol** 3.125 mg bid → 25 mg bid; or **Bisoprolol** 1.25 mg daily → 10 mg) | COPERNICUS, MERIT‑HF, CIBIS‑II showed ↓ mortality. Start low, double every 2‑4 weeks as tolerated; watch for bradycardia, hypotension, and transient worsening of HF symptoms. | | **3. MRA** | **Spironolactone** 12.5‑25 mg po daily → 25‑50 mg (target) (or **Eplerenone** 25 mg po daily → 50 mg) | RALES (spironolactone) ↓ mortality by 30 % in NYHA III–IV; EMPHASIS‑HF (eplerenone) similar benefit in NYHA II–III. Must check K⁺ < 5.0 mmol/L and eGFR > 30 mL/min before initiation; repeat labs in 1‑2 weeks. | | **4. SGLT2‑inhibitor (HF & diabetes)** | **Dapagliflozin** 10 mg po daily **or** **Empagliflozin** 10 mg po daily | DAPA‑HF & EMPEROR‑Reduced: ↓ CV death/HF hospitalisation by ≈ 25 % irrespective of diabetes status. Also improves glycaemic control (A1c ↓ ≈ 0.5‑0.7 %). No dose adjustment needed for eGFR ≥ 30 mL/min. | | **5. Loop diuretic (symptom relief)** | **Furosemide** 20‑40 mg po daily (or IV bolus) → titrate to euvolemia | Needed now because she has bibasilar crackles and peripheral edema. Start low, adjust based on weight, urine output, and renal function. | | **6. Background therapy** | **Metformin** 500‑1000 mg bid (continue if eGFR ≥ 30) | Safe; may be reduced if renal function falls. | | **7. Optional/adjunct** | **GLP‑1‑RA** (e.g., semaglutide weekly) if A1c remains > 7 % after SGLT2‑i and sulfonylurea reduction; provides CV benefit without worsening HF. | Not required for HF but helpful for diabetes and ASCVD risk. | **Putting it together (first ≈ 2 weeks)** | Day 0‑2 | • Hold ACE‑I (if on) → start **furosemide** 20 mg PO q12h (or IV if needed).
• Check baseline labs: Na⁺, K⁺, creatinine/eGFR, CBC, A1c. | | Day 3‑7 | • Initiate **sacubitril/valsartan** 24/26 mg BID (if no ACE‑I) **or** start **losartan** 25‑50 mg daily if ARNI not possible.
• Start **dapagliflozin** 10 mg daily (or empagliflozin). | | Week 2 | • Add **β‑blocker** (metoprolol succinate 12.5 mg daily). Titrate every 2 weeks as tolerated. | | Week 4‑6 | • If K⁺ < 5 mmol/L and eGFR > 30, add **spironolactone** 12.5‑25 mg daily; uptitrate to 25‑50 mg. | | Ongoing | • Re‑check labs after each titration step (K⁺, Cr).
• Monitor weight, symptoms, blood pressure, heart rate.
• Adjust diuretic dose to maintain euvolemia.
• Review glucose logs; consider tapering **glipizide** (e.g., halve dose) once SGLT2‑i is stable. | --- ## 2. **Glycaemic‑control considerations** 1. **SGLT2‑inhibitor as cornerstone** * Lowers A1c modestly, but the primary benefit is HF‑related (↓ hospitalisations, ↓ CV death). * Works even when eGFR is 30‑45 mL/min (no dose reduction needed until < 30). 2. **Metformin** * Continue if eGFR ≥ 30 mL/min/1.73 m² and no severe HF decompensation. Hold during acute renal injury or when diuretic‑induced dehydration occurs. 3. **Sulfonylurea (glipizide)** * Increases hypoglycaemia risk, especially when β‑blocker therapy may mask symptoms. After starting an SGLT2‑i, A1c often falls 0.5‑0.7 %; you can **reduce glipizide dose by 50 %** or stop it altogether, aiming for A1c 7‑7.5 % (ADA target for most > 65 y). 4. **Potential need for additional agents** * If A1c remains > 8 % after SGLT2‑i and metformin, a **GLP‑1‑RA** (semaglutide, dulaglutide) is preferred over adding another sulfonylurea or insulin because it provides CV benefit without fluid retention. 5. **Monitoring for SGLT2‑i adverse effects** * **Genital mycotic infections** – counsel on hygiene; treat promptly. * **Euglycaemic DKA** – rare but higher risk with low carbohydrate intake, alcohol excess, or acute illness; educate on “sick‑day” rule (temporarily stop SGLT2‑i if vomiting/poor oral intake). * **Volume depletion** – especially when combined with loop diuretics; check orthostatic vitals and consider a modest reduction in diuretic dose if symptomatic hypotension develops. --- ## 3. **Key drug‑drug interaction / safety checks** | Interaction | Why it matters | Practical step | |-------------|----------------|----------------| | **ARNI + ACE‑I** | Duplicate RAAS blockade → angioedema, hyperkalaemia. | If patient is on an ACE‑I, discontinue **and wait 36 h** before starting sacubitril/valsartan. | | **ARNI / ACE‑I / ARB + MRA** | ↑ serum K⁺, risk of hyperkalaemia & renal dysfunction. | Check K⁺ and Cr at baseline, then 1‑2 weeks after MRA start, then every 3‑6 months. Keep K⁺ < 5.0 mmol/L. | | **β‑Blocker + Glipizide** | β‑blocker may blunt adrenergic warning signs of hypoglycaemia. | Reduce glipizide dose; advise patient to check glucose before meals and recognize non‑adrenergic symptoms (e.g., sweating). | | **Loop diuretic + ACE‑I/ARNI** | Additive drop in GFR/​BP; risk of AKI. | Start diuretic at low dose, monitor creatinine and BP within 1‑2 weeks of any dose change. | | **Metformin + acute HF decompensation** | Risk of lactic acidosis if renal perfusion falls. | Hold metformin during any hospitalization for HF exacerbation or when eGFR falls < 30. | | **Statin + high‑dose spironolactone** | Minimal interaction; just monitor CK if muscle symptoms. | No dose adjustment needed. | | **SGLT2‑i + loop diuretic** | Additive diuresis → volume depletion. | Counsel on adequate oral intake; consider a modest diuretic dose reduction if symptomatic hypotension or > 2 kg weight loss in a week. | --- ## 4. **Follow‑up & titration schedule (practical template)** | Time | Action | Labs / vitals | |------|--------|---------------| | **Baseline** | CBC, BMP, K⁺, Cr, eGFR, LFTs, BNP, A1c, weight, BP, HR | – | | **Day 3‑7** | Start sacubitril/valsartan **and** dapagliflozin. | Re‑check K⁺/Cr at day 7 (especially if on ACE‑I → wash‑out). | | **Week 2** | Initiate β‑blocker (metoprolol succinate 12.5 mg). | BP ≥ 90/60, HR ≥ 50, no symptomatic bradycardia. | | **Week 4** | Add spironolactone (if labs OK). | K⁺, Cr. | | **Week 6‑8** | Up‑titrate each agent toward target (ARNI 97/103 mg bid, β‑blocker 200 mg metoprolol, MRA 25‑50 mg). | Repeat BMP, BNP, weight, NYHA class. | | **Every 3‑6 months** | Review HF symptoms, renal function, electrolytes, A1c, medication adherence. | Adjust diuretic, consider GLP‑1‑RA if A1c > 7.5 %. | --- ### Bottom line for this patient 1. **Start disease‑modifying HFrEF therapy**: - **Sacubitril/valsartan** (after ACE‑I wash‑out) **or** an ARB if ARNI not tolerated. - **β‑blocker** (metoprolol succinate, carvedilol, or bisoprolol), titrated slowly. - **Spironolactone** (MRA) once potassium and renal function are acceptable. - **SGLT2‑inhibitor** (dapagliflozin or empagliflozin) – treats both HF and diabetes. - **Loop diuretic** for current congestion. 2. **Adjust diabetes regimen**: keep metformin (if eGFR ≥ 30), add SGLT2‑i, **reduce or stop glipizide** to avoid hypoglycaemia, and consider a GLP‑1‑RA later if A1c target not met. 3. **Monitor** renal function, electrolytes, blood pressure, heart rate, weight, and glucose closely during titration; educate the patient on signs of volume depletion, hyper‑/hypokalaemia, and euglycaemic DKA. Following this evidence‑based, guideline‑concordant approach will address both her reduced‑ejection‑fraction heart failure and her type‑2 diabetes while minimizing adverse interactions.

items.question:
You are a third‑year internal medicine resident covering a busy urban teaching hospital. A 68‑year‑old man with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (GOLD stage III), hypertension, and type 2 diabetes mellitus presents to the emergency department with a 4‑hour history of sudden onset, severe, tearing chest pain radiating to his back. He describes the pain as “sharp as a knife” and rates it 9/10. He is diaphoretic, appears anxious, and is using accessory muscles to breathe. Vital signs: BP 170/95 mmHg (right arm), 165/92 mmHg (left arm), HR 112 bpm, RR 24 /min, SpO₂ 92 % on room air, temperature 36.8 °C. Physical exam reveals a new, harsh, early‑diastolic murmur best heard at the left sternal border, and a faint, continuous abdominal bruit over the epigastrium. Neurologic exam is non‑focal. Bedside transthoracic echocardiography shows a dilated ascending aorta with an intimal flap consistent with a Type A aortic dissection. Laboratory studies are notable for hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL, leukocytes 14 × 10⁹/L, creatinine 1.4 mg/dL (baseline 1.0 mg/dL), and D‑dimer 2,500 ng/mL. The CT angiogram of the chest confirms a Stanford Type A dissection extending from the aortic root to the proximal abdominal aorta, with involvement of the brachiocephalic and left subclavian arteries but no evidence of pericardial effusion.

Given this presentation, answer the following:

1. What are the immediate medical management steps you should initiate before definitive surgical repair? List them in order of priority, including target blood pressure and heart‑rate goals, pharmacologic agents, and monitoring requirements.
2. Identify two potential complications of a Type A aortic dissection that must be actively surveilled in the first 24 hours after admission, and describe the bedside or imaging modalities you would use to detect them.
3. The patient’s creatinine is mildly elevated. Discuss how this influences your choice of anticoagulation or antiplatelet therapy, if any, in the peri‑operative period.

Provide concise, evidence‑based answers (no more than 150 words per sub‑question). Cite current guideline recommendations (e.g., 2023 ESC, 2022 AHA/ACC) where applicable.
items.answer:
**1. Immediate medical management (ordered by priority)** | Priority | Action | Target / Details | Recommended agents & monitoring | |----------|--------|------------------|----------------------------------| | **A. Rapid assessment & analgesia** | • 2‑IV large‑bore (≥14 G) lines
• 100 % O₂ (titrate to SpO₂ ≥ 94 %)
• IV fentanyl 1–2 µg/kg bolus, then infusion 25–50 µg hr⁻¹ | Pain score ≤ 3 | Continuous pulse‑ox, cardiac rhythm, arterial line (if possible) | | **B. Blood‑pressure & heart‑rate control** | • Goal SBP ≤ 120 mm Hg (or MAP ≤ 65 mm Hg) **and** HR < 60 bpm as soon as possible, without causing hypotension | • First‑line: **Esmolol** 50 µg kg⁻¹ min⁻¹ → titrate to HR < 60 (max 300 µg kg⁻¹ min⁻¹).
• If SBP remains > 120 mm Hg after HR control, add **Sodium nitroprusside** 0.3‑5 µg kg⁻¹ min⁻¹ (or nicardipine 5 mg hr⁻¹ IV).
• Avoid rapid‑acting ACE‑I/ARBs as sole agents. | Continuous arterial pressure line, ECG, urine output ≥ 0.5 mL kg⁻¹ hr⁻¹. | | **C. Additional pharmacologic adjuncts** | • **Morphine** (if pain persists) < 5 mg IV q5‑10 min.
• **Beta‑blocker** (long‑acting) e.g., metoprolol succinate 25 mg PO q12 h once stable.
• **Statin** (if not already on) 40 mg atorvastatin PO (pleiotropic benefit). | Maintain HR < 60 bpm; avoid reflex tachycardia. | | **D. Preparation for surgery** | • Type‑and‑cross, keep patient NPO.
• Reverse anticoagulation if given (see #3).
• Notify cardiothoracic team, OR, perfusion. | Document time of symptom onset, hemodynamics, labs. | | **E. Monitoring** | • ICU bed, continuous ECG, arterial line, central venous pressure if placed, serial labs (CBC, BMP, lactate, troponin).
• Repeat TEE or CT if clinical change. | | *Guideline basis*: ESC 2023 “Aortic Diseases” and AHA/ACC 2022 “Management of Aortic Dissection” recommend SBP ≤ 120 mm Hg and HR < 60 bpm, β‑blockade first, then vasodilator if needed, and immediate analgesia/ICU care. --- **2. Two early complications to surveil (first 24 h)** | Complication | Why it matters | Surveillance modality ( bedside / imaging ) | |--------------|----------------|----------------------------------------------| | **Cardiac tamponade** (rupture into pericardium) | Can cause sudden hemodynamic collapse; mortality > 50 % if untreated. | • bedside **transthoracic echocardiography (TTE)** every 4–6 h or with any BP drop.
• If TTE equivocal, **urgent transesophageal echo (TEE)** or repeat CT angiogram. | | **Malperfusion syndrome** (organ ischemia – e.g., renal, mesenteric, spinal, limb) | Extent of branch‑vessel involvement predicts early morbidity; renal dysfunction already present. | • **Serial serum lactate, creatinine, CK‑MB, and urine output** every 6 h.
• **Duplex ultrasound** of peripheral pulses if limb ischemia suspected.
• **CT angiography** (or bedside TEE for visceral branches) if new abdominal pain, rising lactate, or oliguria. | Both complications are highlighted in ESC 2023 Class I recommendations for continuous hemodynamic and imaging surveillance in the first 24 h. --- **3. Impact of mild renal impairment on peri‑operative antithrombotic strategy** - **Anticoagulation**: Routine pre‑operative anticoagulation is **not indicated** for acute Type A dissection (guidelines give Class III–Harm). If the patient is already on a DOAC or warfarin for another indication, **hold** the agent; reverse warfarin with vitamin K (10 mg) and consider PCC if INR > 2.5. DOACs can be held ≥ 24 h; renal clearance (creatinine clearance ≈ 45 mL/min) may prolong half‑life, so give **idarucizumab** (for dabigatran) or **andexanet alfa** (for factor‑Xa inhibitors) only if bleeding risk is imminent. - **Antiplatelet therapy**: No routine antiplatelet is required pre‑op. If the patient has coronary disease requiring aspirin, a **single low‑dose aspirin (81 mg)** may be continued; it has minimal renal impact. Clopidogrel or other P2Y12 inhibitors should be **held** 5‑7 days pre‑op because they increase intra‑operative bleeding and have no proven benefit in dissection. Thus, with creatinine 1.4 mg/dL (eGFR ≈ 45 mL/min), avoid nephrotoxic anticoagulants and limit antiplatelet exposure; focus on β‑blockade and vasodilators instead. *Guideline citations*: AHA/ACC 2022 Class III (no anticoagulation) and ESC 2023 Class I (avoid routine antiplatelet/anticoag unless other indication).

items.question:
You are an emergency physician in a rural hospital in Canada. A 28-year-old male construction worker is brought in after a fall from a 3‑meter scaffold. He is alert but complains of severe neck pain and paresthesias in both hands. Vital signs: BP 130/85 mmHg, HR 102 bpm, RR 22 breaths/min, SpO₂ 96% on room air. There is a visible step-off over the C5 spinous process, and his cervical range of motion is limited by pain. No obvious external wounds. Provide a concise assessment plan that includes:
1. Immediate stabilization steps and imaging priorities.
2. Key neurological examination elements to document.
3. Differential diagnosis for his neck injury.
4. Initial management recommendations pending definitive imaging.
items.answer:
**28‑year‑old male – fall from 3 m, severe neck pain, bilateral hand paresthesias, step‑off at C5 spinous process** *Rural Canadian ED – limited immediate resources, need to protect the cervical spine while arranging definitive imaging.* --- ## 1. Immediate stabilization & imaging priorities | Action | Rationale / How‑to | |--------|---------------------| | **C‑spine immobilisation** | • Apply a rigid cervical collar (e.g., Aspen®).
• Secure with head‑block and tape to prevent motion.
• If collar unavailable, use a stacked‑board/foam “sandwich” technique. | | **Log‑roll with manual in‑line traction** | Maintain neutral alignment while moving to a backboard or stretcher for transport. | | **Two large‑bore IVs** | 18‑gauge in each arm; give crystalloid (normal saline 1 L) to maintain euvolemia. | | **O₂ & monitoring** | Continue pulse‑ox, cardiac monitor, non‑invasive BP; keep SpO₂ ≥ 94 %. | | **Analgesia (non‑sedating)** | IV paracetamol 1 g (or PO if tolerating) ± low‑dose fentanyl 25‑50 µg titrated; avoid deep sedation until spine cleared. | | **NPO & gastric protection** | Keep NPO; give IV pantoprazole 40 mg q24h (stress‑ulcer prophylaxis). | | **Imaging – first line** | **CT cervical spine (multidetector, ≤1 mm slices) from occiput to T2** – rapid, highly sensitive for bony injury, can be performed on‑site. | | **If CT shows fracture/dislocation or high‑risk mechanism** | Arrange **MRI of the cervical spine** (T1/T2/STIR) as soon as possible (often at the next regional centre) to evaluate ligamentous injury, cord edema/contusion, and disc/soft‑tissue damage. | | **If CT is negative but neurologic deficit persists** | Still obtain MRI (central cord or ligamentous injury can be occult on CT). | | **Transfer considerations** | If imaging suggests unstable fracture, cord compression, or progressive neuro deficit, coordinate rapid transfer to a tertiary centre with neurosurgical spine capability. | --- ## 2. Key neurological examination elements to document | Domain | Specific items (bilateral) | |--------|----------------------------| | **Mental status** | Alert, oriented ×3; GCS 15. | | **Motor strength** | MRC grade 0‑5 for C5‑T1 myotomes (deltoid, biceps, wrist extensors, triceps, hand intrinsic). | | **Sensory** | Light touch & pinprick for dermatomes C4‑T1 (shoulder, lateral arm, forearm, dorsal/volar hand). Note any “stocking‑glove” pattern. | | **Reflexes** | Biceps (C5‑6), triceps (C7), brachioradialis, finger flexor (C8‑T1), Hoffmann sign, Babinski. | | **Coordination** | Finger‑nose, rapid alternating movements (if cooperative). | | **Upper‑extremity proprioception** | Position sense in fingers. | | **Lower‑extremity exam** | Motor, sensory, reflexes (to rule out more extensive cord injury). | | **Rectal tone & anal wink** | Assess sacral sparing; document presence/absence. | | **Autonomic signs** | Blood pressure variability, urinary retention, bowel function. | | **Pain localisation** | Exact level of maximal tenderness / step‑off. | | **Document baseline** | Photograph (if consent) or sketch the step‑off; record time of exam. | *All findings should be recorded verbatim (e.g., “5/5 strength in deltoids, 4/5 in wrist extensors, decreased pinprick in C6‑C8 dermatomes bilaterally”).* --- ## 3. Differential diagnosis for his neck injury | Category | Specific entities (most likely → less likely) | |----------|----------------------------------------------| | **Bony injury** | • **C5 spinous‑process fracture** (avulsion or compression)
• **Cervical facet fracture/dislocation** (C4‑C5, C5‑C6)
• **Compression burst fracture** of C5 vertebral body
• **Hangman’s fracture** (C2) – less likely given step‑off at C5 | | **Ligamentous injury** | • **Posterior ligament complex (PLC) rupture**
• **Anterior longitudinal ligament tear**
• **Interspinous ligament disruption** | | **Spinal cord/neurologic injury** | • **Central cord syndrome** (common in falls with hand involvement)
• **Brown‑Séquard** (if unilateral signs)
• **Spinal cord contusion/edema**
• **Incomplete cervical cord injury (ASIA C/D)** | | **Nerve‑root / brachial plexus injury** | • **C5–C8 radiculopathy** from foraminal compromise
• **Traumatic brachial plexus stretch** (though mechanism less typical) | | **Soft‑tissue / vascular** | • **Prevertebral hematoma**
• **Vertebral artery injury** (if transverse foramen involvement)
• **Cervical muscle strain/contusion** | | **Non‑spinal** | • **Cervical rib or thoracic outlet syndrome** – unlikely acutely
• **Peripheral neuropathy** – ruled out by acute mechanism | --- ## 4. Initial management recommendations pending definitive imaging 1. **Maintain rigid cervical immobilisation** until a stable spine is confirmed (or definitive surgical fixation is performed). 2. **Hemodynamic optimisation** – target MAP ≥ 85 mmHg for suspected cord injury (use crystalloid bolus ± vasopressor if needed). 3. **Avoid high‑dose steroids** – current Canadian and international guidelines (e.g., CANS, AANS) do **not** recommend routine methylprednisolone for acute traumatic spinal cord injury. 4. **Analgesia** – give acetaminophen ± low‑dose opioid; consider a short‑acting muscle relaxant (e.g., baclofen 10 mg PO) if severe spasms develop. 5. **Nausea prophylaxis** – ondansetron 4 mg IV if needed (prevents vomiting‑related neck movement). 6. **Serial neurological checks** – every 15 min for the first hour, then q30 min; document any change promptly. 7. **Consultations** – * **Neurosurgery/orthopaedic spine** (via phone/tele‑consult) once imaging is obtained. * **Radiology** – expedite CT; arrange MRI slot at nearest centre if CT suggests instability or cord compromise. * **Transport team** – if transfer required, ensure cervical collar remains in place and that the receiving facility is prepared for possible surgical decompression. 8. **Patient & family communication** – explain the need for immobilisation, imaging plan, and possible outcomes; obtain consent for transfer if indicated. 9. **Documentation** – time‑stamp all interventions, vital signs, neuro exams, and imaging orders. --- **Bottom line:** - **Immobilise, monitor, and obtain a rapid CT cervical spine**. - **Perform a focused, reproducible neuro exam** and repeat it frequently. - **Treat as an unstable cervical spine until proven otherwise** (maintain MAP ≥ 85 mmHg, analgesia, NPO). - **Escalate to MRI and neurosurgical consultation** based on CT findings or persistent deficits, and arrange transfer if definitive care exceeds local capability.

items.question:
You are an emergency physician in a rural district hospital in Southeast Asia. A 28‑year‑old pregnant woman at 30 weeks gestation presents with sudden onset of severe, throbbing headache, visual disturbances (blurred vision and occasional flashes), and nausea. She reports no prior hypertension, but she has a history of mild asthma. Vital signs: BP 170/110 mmHg, HR 96 bpm, RR 20/min, SpO₂ 98% on room air, temperature 37.2 °C. Physical exam reveals a fundoscopic grade III papilledema, brisk deep tendon reflexes, and mild peripheral edema. Urine dipstick is +2 protein. The fetal heart rate is 150 bpm with moderate variability.

1. What is the most likely diagnosis and what are the key clinical criteria that support it?
2. Outline the immediate stabilization steps for both mother and fetus, including pharmacologic and non‑pharmacologic interventions that are feasible in a resource‑limited setting.
3. Which antihypertensive agents are preferred for acute blood pressure control in severe pre‑eclampsia, and why?
4. What are the indications for emergent delivery in this scenario, and what mode of delivery would be most appropriate given the gestational age and maternal condition?
5. Provide a brief follow‑up plan for postpartum monitoring and counseling for this patient.

items.question: I am an emergency physician at a tertiary care center and see a 34-year-old male who was brought in after a high‑speed motorbike collision. He is alert, oriented, and complains of severe abdominal pain radiating to his back. Vital signs: BP 100/60 mmHg, HR 118 bpm, RR 22/min, SpO₂ 98% on room air, Temp 37.2 °C. Physical exam reveals a tender, distended abdomen with guarding, especially in the left flank, and diminished bowel sounds. FAST exam is positive for free fluid in the left upper quadrant and perisplenic area. Labs show hemoglobin 12 g/dL, hematocrit 36%, lactate 3.2 mmol/L, and normal renal function. What is the most appropriate next step in management, and what are the key considerations for this patient’s hemodynamic and imaging evaluation?
items.answer:
**Short answer:**  
Give the patient a rapid “damage‑control” resuscitation (type‑and‑cross, give blood products/large‑bore crystalloid as needed, keep SBP ≈ 90‑100 mm Hg) and, because he is *borderline* but still hemodynamically “stable,” proceed immediately to a **contrast‑enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis** (pan‑scan) to define the source of the left‑upper‑quadrant free fluid (splenic vs. pancreatic vs. retroperitoneal injury).  

If at any point his blood pressure falls below the 90‑mm Hg threshold, becomes refractory to fluids/blood, or his mental status deteriorates, the plan changes to **emergent operative control** (laparotomy or, if a splenic injury is suspected and the patient is still relatively stable, possible interventional radiology embolization after a short “stop‑the‑bleed” laparotomy).

---

## Why CT is the next best step

| Finding | Interpretation | Implication for management |
|---------|----------------|----------------------------|
| **Alert, oriented, SpO₂ 98 %** | No airway or severe respiratory compromise. | Focus on circulatory and abdominal evaluation. |
| **BP 100/60 mm Hg, HR 118 bpm** | Borderline hypotension with compensatory tachycardia → *Class II–III* hemorrhagic shock. Still above the “critical” 90‑mm Hg trigger for immediate operative bypass. |
| **FAST +** (free fluid in LUQ/perisplenic) | Confirms intra‑abdominal fluid, most likely splenic or left renal injury. | Needs an anatomic definition; FAST alone cannot grade injury or guide non‑operative vs. operative decision. |
| **Lactate 3.2 mmol/L** | Early sign of tissue hypoperfusion. | Trend lactate while resuscitating; supports need for rapid control of bleeding. |
| **Hemoglobin 12 g/dL** | May be “normal” because acute bleed has not yet diluted. | Do not rely on Hgb to rule out major hemorrhage. |
| **No other obvious source of bleeding** | Isolated left‑upper‑quadrant fluid → splenic or left renal injury most likely. | CT will differentiate and grade the injury. |

Because the patient meets **the hemodynamic definition of “stable enough for CT”** (SBP > 90 mm Hg, no ongoing massive transfusion requirement, mental status intact), the **contrast‑enhanced CT abdomen/pelvis** is the most efficient way to:

1. **Identify the injured organ** (splenic laceration, subcapsular hematoma, pancreatic transection, left renal injury, mesenteric tear, etc.).
2. **Grade the injury** (American Association for the Surgery of Trauma – AAST grades). This grading drives the decision between non‑operative management (NOM), angio‑embolization, or operative repair.
3. **Detect active contrast extravasation** (“blush”) that predicts ongoing arterial bleeding and may prompt immediate IR embolization or operative control even if the patient is still “stable.”

---

## Step‑by‑step management pathway in the ED

1. **Primary survey & resuscitation**  
   - **Airway:** Patent, protect if needed (no sign of compromise).  
   - **Breathing:** 98 % on room air – give supplemental O₂ if SpO₂ falls <94 %.  
   - **Circulation:**  
     - Place two large‑bore (16‑14 G) IVs (already done for FAST).  
     - **Type & crossmatch** immediately; request **O‑negative PRBC** if cross‑matched blood not yet available.  
     - **Permissive hypotension**: target SBP ≈ 90‑100 mm Hg (MAP ≈ 65 mm Hg) until source control is achieved, unless there is a known traumatic brain injury (TBI) where higher MAP is required.  
     - Give **1 L crystalloid** (or a balanced solution such as Plasma‑Lyte) **only if MAP < 65 mm Hg**; otherwise go straight to blood products (PRBC : FFP : PLT ≈ 1 : 1 : 1) if you suspect ongoing hemorrhage.  
     - **Tranexamic acid (TXA):** 1 g IV over 10 min followed by 1 g over 8 h, **if < 3 h** from injury (per CRASH‑2).  
   - **Adjuncts:** Foley catheter (monitor urine output), nasogastric tube (decompress if needed), analgesia (ketamine or short‑acting opioid).

2. **Re‑evaluate hemodynamics after the first resuscitative bolus**  
   - If SBP remains < 90 mm Hg despite 1 L crystalloid + 1 unit PRBC, **activate massive‑transfusion protocol (MTP)** and **take the patient directly to the OR** (or hybrid OR if IR is available).  
   - If SBP stabilizes at 95‑110 mm Hg, HR improves (< 110), lactate begins to trend down → proceed to imaging.

3. **Imaging**  
   - **CT protocol:** Whole‑body trauma pan‑scan (head, cervical spine, chest, abdomen, pelvis) **with arterial and portal‑venous phases**. For isolated abdominal trauma, a **triphasic abdomen/pelvis** (arterial, portal, delayed) is sufficient.  
   - **Contra‑indications:** Uncontrolled hypotension, severe contrast allergy, severe renal failure (not present).  
   - **If CT not feasible** (e.g., patient decompensates while in scanner) → **stop the scan** and go to the OR.

4. **Interpret CT – decision algorithm**  

   - **Splenic injury**  
     - **AAST Grade I‑II, no active blush, hemodynamically stable** → non‑operative management (observation, serial abdominal exams, repeat Hgb, repeat FAST).  
     - **AAST Grade III‑IV, or any grade with active contrast extravasation** → consider **angiographic embolization** if IR is immediately available and the patient remains stable.  
     - **AAST Grade V, or blush with hemodynamic instability** → **damage‑control laparotomy** (splenectomy or splenorrhaphy).  

   - **Pancreatic or duodenal injury** (less common in this scenario) → operative or endoscopic depending on grade and stability.  

   - **Renal injury** → similar NOM vs. embolization vs. nephrectomy algorithm.

5. **Post‑CT care**  
   - Admit to **level‑1 trauma ICU**.  
   - Continue **balanced resuscitation**, maintain MAP ≥ 65 mm Hg, urine output ≥ 0.5 mL/kg/h.  
   - Serial **lactate, Hgb**, and **repeat FAST** every 6–8 h or sooner if the exam changes.  
   - **Analgesia** (ketamine infusion, low‑dose opioids) while avoiding oversedation that masks peritonitis.  
   - **Antibiotics** only if there is a hollow‑viscus injury or operative intervention.  

---

## Key hemodynamic considerations for this patient

| Issue | Why it matters | Practical tip |
|-------|----------------|---------------|
| **Permissive hypotension** | Prevents dislodging clots and worsening hemorrhage. | Keep SBP ≈ 90‑100 mm Hg (MAP ≈ 65) until definitive control. |
| **Early blood product use** | Crystalloid alone dilutes clotting factors and raises intra‑abdominal pressure. | If suspicion for > 1500 mL blood loss, give **PRBC + FFP + Platelets** in a 1:1:1 ratio (or use whole blood if available). |
| **TXA timing** | Reduces mortality when given < 3 h after injury. | 1 g bolus now, then 1 g over 8 h. |
| **Lactate trend** | Real‑time surrogate for tissue perfusion. | Re‑check lactate every 30‑60 min; falling trend = adequate resuscitation. |
| **Abdominal compartment syndrome (ACS)** | Massive fluid resuscitation + intra‑abdominal bleed can raise intra‑abdominal pressure (IAP). | Monitor bladder pressure if > 12 mm Hg and consider decompressive laparotomy if IAP > 20 mm Hg with organ dysfunction. |
| **Coagulopathy** | Traumatic bleeding coagulopathy can develop early. | Give plasma & platelets early; consider point‑of‑care viscoelastic testing (TEG/ROTEM) if available. |
| **Renal perfusion** | Even with normal baseline creatinine, hypoperfusion can precipitate AKI. | Maintain MAP ≥ 65 mm Hg, avoid nephrotoxic drugs, monitor urine output. |

---

## Key imaging considerations

1. **CT timing** – Must be done **after initial resuscitation** but **before the patient becomes unstable**. In most trauma centers the “CT‑ready” time is < 15 min from decision to image.
2. **Contrast dose** – 100–120 mL of non‑ionic iodinated contrast (e.g., iohexol 350 mg I/mL) injected at 3–4 mL/s, followed by a saline flush. Use a **dual‑phase protocol** for the abdomen to capture arterial blush.
3. **Radiation vs. benefit** – In a 34‑year‑old the benefit of delineating a potentially splenic injury far outweighs radiation risk, especially when operative decision hinges on CT grade.
4. **Alternative if CT unavailable** – **Diagnostic peritoneal lavage (DPL)** or repeat FAST combined with serial exams can be used, but they do not grade injury; they only tell you “blood present.” In a hemodynamically borderline patient, DPL may push you straight to laparotomy.
5. **Hybrid OR** – Some centers have a **“CT‑to‑OR”** suite where the patient can be scanned and, if active bleeding is seen, taken straight to the OR/IR without moving the table. If your institution has this capability, use it.

---

## Bottom line for this case

- **Resuscitate** aggressively but with permissive hypotension (type‑and‑cross, give blood products, TXA).  
- **Re‑assess** after the first bolus; if still borderline but stable, **go to contrast‑enhanced CT** (pan‑scan) to define the injury.  
- **If CT shows a low‑grade splenic injury without blush** → non‑operative observation in ICU.  
- **If CT shows a high‑grade injury or active contrast extravasation** → **angiographic embolization** (if IR available) or **damage‑control laparotomy** if the patient deteriorates.  

All of this should be done while **continuously monitoring vitals, lactate, urine output, and repeat FAST** to catch any early decompensation.

items.question: I am a cardiology fellow in a community hospital managing a 55-year-old woman with newly diagnosed hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) who presents with exertional dyspnea and presyncope. Echocardiography shows a maximal left ventricular wall thickness of 22 mm, a left atrial volume index of 45 mL/m², and a resting left ventricular outflow tract gradient of 35 mmHg that increases to 70 mmHg with Valsalva. She has a family history of sudden cardiac death (father at age 48) and carries a pathogenic MYH7 mutation. The patient is currently on metoprolol succinate 100 mg daily but continues to have symptoms. What are the next evidence‑based therapeutic steps you would recommend (including pharmacologic options, consideration of septal reduction therapy, and device therapy), and what specific criteria would guide each decision? Please provide a concise, step‑wise answer.
items.answer:
**Step‑wise, evidence‑based plan for a 55‑year‑old woman with symptomatic HCM, high LVOT gradient, and high‑risk SCD profile** | Step | What to do | How to decide (criteria) | Key references / guideline points | |------|------------|--------------------------|------------------------------------| | **1. Optimize medical therapy** | a) **Increase β‑blocker dose** (metoprolol succinate 150‑200 mg daily) or switch to an equivalent long‑acting β‑blocker (e.g., atenolol 100 mg).
b) **Add negative inotrope** if gradient remains ≥ 50 mmHg and symptoms persist: **disopyramide** 150‑300 mg PO q8h (start low, monitor QT).
c) **If β‑blocker intolerant or insufficient**, consider **non‑dihydropyridine calcium‑channel blocker** (verapamil 240 mg daily or diltiazem 240‑300 mg daily). | • Resting gradient ≥ 30 mmHg **or** provoked ≥ 50 mmHg with symptoms despite β‑blocker.
• No contraindication to higher β‑blocker dose (e.g., severe asthma, bradycardia <50 bpm, SBP <90 mmHg).
• Disopyramide only if QTc <470 ms and no significant conduction disease. | 2020 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline for HCM (class I, level B); 2022 ESC HCM Guideline (class I, level B). | | **2. Re‑assess after 4–6 weeks** | Repeat symptom questionnaire (NYHA class), office BP/HR, and **repeat echo or Doppler** to document resting and provoked LVOT gradient. | • Persistent gradient ≥ 50 mmHg **and** NYHA III–IV (or II with marked limitation) → move to septal reduction.
