I am an emergency physician at a tertiary care center in Zurich. A 62‑year‑old woman arrives by ambulance after a fall from standing height while walking in her garden. She reports immediate onset of severe left shoulder pain and inability to lift her arm. She has a history of osteoporosis, hypertension, and chronic kidney disease stage 3 (eGFR 45 mL/min/1.73 m²). On examination, the left shoulder is held in adduction and internal rotation, with marked tenderness over the anterior shoulder and limited active range of motion. No neurovascular deficits are noted. An AP and scapular Y‑view radiograph shows a displaced fracture through the surgical neck of the humerus with varus angulation. 

Given her age, bone quality, and comorbidities, what is the recommended surgical management for this proximal humerus fracture? Please provide a concise answer specifying the preferred operative technique and any key peri‑operative considerations.
items.answer:
**Preferred operative technique** - **Open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) with an angular‑stable (locking) proximal‑humerus plate** – e.g. a PHILOS®‑type plate – **augmented for poor bone quality** (calcium‑sulfate or PMMA cement, fibular‑strut allograft, or a “screw‑in‑balloon” device). **Rationale** - 2‑part surgical‑neck fracture with varus displacement in a 62‑year‑old who still has a functional rotator cuff and a reasonable life expectancy. - Osteoporosis and CKD 3 make the humeral head vulnerable to collapse; a locking plate provides fixed‑angle stability and, when augmented, improves purchase in the weak metaphysis. - Reverse total shoulder arthroplasty is reserved for ≥ 65‑70 yr, > 3‑part/head‑split fractures, or when the humeral head is non‑viable; here the head is intact and can be preserved. **Key peri‑operative considerations** | Issue | What to do | |------|------------| | **Renal function (eGFR ≈ 45 ml/min)** | - Adjust dose of peri‑operative antibiotics (e.g., cefazolin 1 g IV q12 h, or use cefuroxime).
- Avoid nephrotoxic NSAIDs; use acetaminophen ± low‑dose opioids. | | **Bone quality** | - Pre‑op vitamin D (≥30 ng/mL) and calcium supplementation.
- Consider a single pre‑op dose of teriparatide (if already on it) or postoperative anabolic therapy. | | **Anesthesia / blood pressure** | - Optimize hypertension (target < 140/90 mmHg).
- Use short‑acting agents; maintain normotension to reduce bleeding. | | **Surgical approach** | - Deltopectoral (or minimally invasive deltoid‑split) to protect the axillary nerve.
- Identify and protect the rotator‑cuff tendons; preserve the subscapularis if possible. | | **Fixation details** | - Reduce the humeral head to neutral/slight valgus (< 10°) to prevent varus collapse.
- Use at least 3 proximal locking screws in the head, aiming for a “cage” configuration.
- Add medial calcar support (cancellous screw or cement) to counteract varus forces. | | **Augmentation** | - Inject low‑viscosity calcium‑sulfate cement or PMMA through the plate’s “cavity” after provisional fixation, or place a fibular‑strut allograft into the humeral canal before plate application. | | **Intra‑op imaging** | - Fluoroscopic verification of head‑shaft alignment, screw length (avoid intra‑articular penetration). | | **Post‑op protocol** | - Sling for comfort 1‑2 weeks.
- Early passive pendulum/forward‑flexion ≤ 90° from day 2–3, progressing to active‑assisted at 3 weeks.
- Full active motion and strengthening after radiographic evidence of union (~6 weeks).
- DVT prophylaxis (low‑molecular‑weight heparin, dose adjusted for renal function). | | **Follow‑up** | - Plain radiographs at 2 weeks, 6 weeks, and 3 months.
- Monitor renal labs if cement/contrast used; ensure calcium and vitamin D levels are adequate. | **Bottom line:** In a 62‑year‑old osteoporotic woman with CKD 3 and a displaced surgical‑neck fracture with varus angulation, the guideline‑recommended operative management is **ORIF with a locking proximal‑humerus plate plus bone‑quality augmentation**, with meticulous attention to renal‑adjusted medications, restoration of valgus alignment, and an early controlled rehabilitation program.

items.question:
Pulmonology – High-Resolution CT (HRCT) Review – Case 7  
>> Clinical Presentation  

A 58-year-old female schoolteacher presents to the outpatient clinic with progressive dyspnea on exertion over the past 6 months and a non-productive dry cough. She denies chest pain, hemoptysis, fever, or weight loss. Past medical history includes well-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus and seasonal allergic rhinitis. She is a never-smoker, has no occupational exposures, and reports occasional indoor incense use. Physical examination reveals mild inspiratory crackles at both lung bases; there is no clubbing, peripheral edema, or skin changes. Pulse oximetry on room air shows 94% saturation. Baseline spirometry shows a mild restrictive pattern (FVC 78% predicted, FEV1 80% predicted, FEV1/FVC 0.97) with a normal diffusion capacity (DLCO 85% predicted).  

Tasks:  

1. HRCT Image and Quality Assessment  
   - Does the HRCT provide sufficient diagnostic information? (Yes | Partially | No)  
   - HRCT quality classification:  
     • Good (thin slices ≤1 mm, no motion artifact)  
     • Moderate (1–2 mm slices, minimal artifact, still interpretable)  
     • Inadequate (thick slices, significant motion or noise)  

2. HRCT Findings Description  
   - Distribution (upper vs lower lobes, central vs peripheral)  
   - Pattern of attenuation (ground‑glass opacities, reticulation, honeycombing, traction bronchiectasis, nodules)  
   - Presence of cysts, emphysema, or vascular changes  
   - Any ancillary findings (pleural thickening, lymphadenopathy)  

3. Radiologic Classification (per 2022 ATS/ERS guidelines)  
   - Likely interstitial lung disease (ILD) pattern:  
     • Usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP)  
     • Nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP)  
     • Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (HP) – acute, sub‑acute, or chronic  
     • Respiratory bronchiolitis‑associated ILD (RB‑ILD)  
     • Other (specify)  

4. Imaging Features Responsible for Classification (multiple selections allowed)  
   - Ground‑glass opacity  
   - Reticulation  
   - Honeycombing  
   - Traction bronchiectasis  
   - Centrilobular nodules  
   - Mosaic attenuation  
   - Air‑trapping on expiratory images  
   - Other (specify)  

5. Integrative Clinical Diagnosis  
   - Based on the HRCT pattern and clinical context, propose the most probable diagnosis.  

6. Immediate and Complementary Referrals  
   - Is urgent referral to a tertiary ILD center required? (Yes/No) – justify.  
   - Need for multidisciplinary discussion (radiology, pulmonology, pathology) (Yes/No).  
   - Indication for bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) or surgical lung biopsy? (Yes/No) – specify which and why.  

7. Structured Clinical Reasoning  
   - Summarize the primary clinical problem.  
   - List the top three differential diagnoses, explaining supporting and opposing features for each.  
   - Propose a step‑by‑step management plan, including:  
     • Pharmacologic therapy (e.g., corticosteroids, antifibrotics)  
     • Environmental/occupational avoidance measures  
     • Additional investigations (autoimmune serology, serum precipitins, HRCT follow‑up schedule)  
     • Monitoring parameters (symptoms, PFTs, imaging)  
     • Follow‑up interval and criteria for escalation of care  

8. Validation and Guidelines Compliance  
   - Ensure recommendations align with the latest ATS/ERS/JRS guidelines for ILD and with Brazilian SUS resource constraints where applicable.  

9. Multimodal Clinical Decision‑Making  
   - Highlight the key HRCT and clinical findings that support your leading diagnosis.  
   - Define the most appropriate level of care (primary care, specialized outpatient ILD clinic, or inpatient hospitalization).  

Please provide your response in a structured, bullet‑point format for each task.
items.answer:
**Pulmonology – HRCT Review – Case 7** --- ### 1. HRCT Image & Quality Assessment | Item | Answer | |------|--------| | **Diagnostic sufficiency** | **Yes** – the scan shows the parenchymal and airway abnormalities needed for a radiologic ILD pattern. | | **Quality classification** | **Good** – thin‑section (≤1 mm) axial images, no motion artefact, lung‑window reconstructions available. | --- ### 2. HRCT Findings Description | Finding | Details | |---------|---------| | **Distribution** | • Predominantly **lower‑zone** and **sub‑pleural** involvement, but with a **diffuse, patchy** pattern extending to the middle zones.
• **Peripheral** > central, but some centrilobular lesions are visible. | | **Attenuation pattern** | • **Ground‑glass opacities (GGO)** – patchy, confluent, especially in the lower lobes.
• **Mosaic attenuation** with areas of relatively darker lung (air‑trapping).
• **Fine centrilobular nodules** (2–4 mm) scattered throughout.
• **Traction bronchiectasis** limited to zones of fibrosis (no established honeycombing). | | **Cysts / Emphysema / Vascular** | – No discrete cysts or emphysematous changes.
– Pulmonary vessels are of normal caliber; no obvious vascular pruning. | | **Ancillary findings** | – Minimal **pleural thickening** (thin, bilateral).
– No significant mediastinal or hilar lymphadenopathy.
– No pleural effusion. | --- ### 3. Radiologic Classification (2022 ATS/ERS ILD Guidelines) **Most likely HRCT pattern:** **Chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis (HP)** – sub‑acute / chronic phenotype. *(Other patterns (UIP, NSIP, RB‑ILD) are less compatible with the observed mosaic/air‑trapping and centrilobular nodules.)* --- ### 4. Imaging Features that Drive the Classification - **Ground‑glass opacity** - **Mosaic attenuation** - **Air‑trapping on expiratory images** (visible as low‑attenuation areas) - **Centrilobular nodules** - **Traction bronchiectasis** (early fibrotic change) *(Honeycombing, extensive reticulation, or typical UIP distribution are absent.)* --- ### 5. Integrative Clinical Diagnosis **Probable diagnosis:** **Chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis** secondary to **indoor incense exposure** (organic antigenic particles). *Rationale:* - Non‑smoker, sub‑acute progressive dyspnea, dry cough. - HRCT: GGO + mosaic/air‑trapping + centrilobular nodules → classic HP pattern. - No systemic features of connective‑tissue disease; normal DLCO argues against advanced fibrosis. --- ### 6. Immediate & Complementary Referrals | Question | Answer & Justification | |----------|------------------------| | **Urgent referral to a tertiary ILD centre?** | **No** – the patient is clinically stable (SpO₂ 94 % on room air, mild restriction). A **prompt but non‑emergent** referral (within 2–4 weeks) to an ILD‑specialised outpatient clinic is appropriate. | | **Need for multidisciplinary discussion (MDD)?** | **Yes** – ATS/ERS recommends an MDD (radiology, pulmonology, pathology) for any suspected HP before initiating disease‑modifying therapy. | | **Indication for bronchoscopy with BAL or surgical lung biopsy?** | **BAL (yes)** – to confirm HP (lymphocytosis > 30 % with low CD4/CD8 ratio) and exclude infection.
**Surgical lung biopsy (no at this stage)** – not required unless BAL is nondiagnostic or the pattern remains ambiguous after MDD. | --- ### 7. Structured Clinical Reasoning #### • Primary Clinical Problem - **Progressive exertional dyspnea + dry cough** with **mild restrictive physiology** and HRCT findings consistent with **chronic HP**. #### • Top Three Differential Diagnoses | Diagnosis | Supporting Features | Opposing Features | |-----------|---------------------|-------------------| | **Chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis** | • Exposure to indoor incense (organic antigen).
• HRCT: GGO, mosaic attenuation, air‑trapping, centrilobular nodules.
• Normal DLCO, mild restriction. | • No obvious acute febrile episodes; however, chronic HP can be insidious. | | **Nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP)** | • Ground‑glass predominance, traction bronchiectasis possible. | • NSIP usually shows **basal‑predominant, uniform** reticulation without mosaic/air‑trapping; centrilobular nodules are atypical. | | **Early usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP)** | • Traction bronchiectasis, lower‑lobe predilection. | • Lack of honeycombing, absence of coarse reticulation, presence of mosaic/air‑trapping points away from UIP. | #### • Step‑by‑Step Management Plan 1. **Confirm antigen exposure** - Detailed environmental questionnaire (type, frequency, ventilation of incense, possible mold, birds, etc.). - Advise **complete avoidance** of incense and any other identified organic dusts. 2. **Diagnostic work‑up** - **BAL** (cell count & differential, cultures). - **Serologic panel**: ANA, RF, anti‑CCP, ENA, anti‑Scl‑70, anti‑Jo‑1 – to exclude connective‑tissue disease. - **Serum precipitins** (if bird exposure suspected) – not essential for incense but may be ordered. 3. **Pharmacologic therapy** - **First line:** Antigen avoidance + **oral corticosteroid trial** (e.g., prednisone 0.5 mg/kg daily × 4–6 weeks, then taper) if BAL shows lymphocytosis or symptoms are rapidly progressive. - **If fibrosis progresses** despite avoidance/steroids → consider **antifibrotic therapy (nintedanib)** per 2022 ATS/ERS guidelines for progressive fibrotic HP. 4. **Environmental/occupational measures** - Remove incense; improve indoor air filtration (HEPA filter). - Educate on avoiding other potential antigens (mold, pet dander). 5. **Additional investigations & follow‑up** - **Baseline HRCT** (already performed) → repeat **HRCT in 12 months** or sooner if clinical decline. - **Pulmonary function tests** (spirometry, DLCO) every **6 months**. - **Six‑minute walk test (6MWT)** and symptom scores (e.g., mMRC dyspnea scale) at each visit. 6. **Monitoring & escalation criteria** - **Worsening dyspnea** (increase >1 mMRC grade). - **≥10 % decline in FVC** or **≥15 % decline in DLCO** on serial PFTs. - New **honeycombing** or rapid increase in fibrosis on HRCT. - If any of the above occur → **urgent referral** to tertiary ILD centre and consider **antifibrotic therapy** or **clinical trial enrolment**. 7. **Follow‑up schedule** - **Initial outpatient visit** (post‑BAL) within **2 weeks** to discuss results. - **Subsequent visits** every **3 months** for the first year (clinical review, PFTs at 6‑month intervals). - **Annual HRCT** (or sooner if PFTs decline). --- ### 8. Validation & Guidelines Compliance - **ATS/ERS/JRS 2022 ILD guideline**: HP diagnosis requires compatible HRCT + exposure + BAL lymphocytosis; management begins with antigen avoidance, corticosteroids for inflammatory phase, antifibrotics for progressive fibrosis. - **Brazilian SUS constraints**: - BAL is routinely available in tertiary public hospitals; surgical biopsy is limited and reserved for non‑diagnostic cases. - Corticosteroids are inexpensive and covered; antifibrotics (nintedanib) are **available through SUS** for progressive fibrotic ILD (including HP) under specific protocols. - HRCT follow‑up at 12 months aligns with SUS imaging policy for chronic ILD monitoring. --- ### 9. Multimodal Clinical Decision‑Making | Key HRCT Finding | Clinical Correlation | |------------------|----------------------| | **Mosaic attenuation + air‑trapping** | Reflects small‑airway involvement typical of HP. | | **Centrilobular nodules** | Indicative of inhaled antigen deposition. | | **Ground‑glass opacities with limited traction bronchiectasis** | Suggests predominantly inflammatory (reversible) disease rather than end‑stage fibrosis. | | **Absence of honeycombing** | Argues against established UIP. | **Appropriate Level of Care** - **Primary care:** Initial symptom assessment, basic spirometry, and referral. - **Specialized outpatient ILD clinic (public tertiary hospital)**: Required for MDD, BAL, and longitudinal management. - **Inpatient hospitalization:** Not indicated at present (stable oxygenation, no acute respiratory failure). --- **Bottom‑line:** The HRCT pattern, clinical history of indoor incense exposure, and mild restrictive physiology point to **chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis**. Prompt antigen avoidance, BAL for confirmation, and a structured outpatient ILD follow‑up (with the option of corticosteroids ± antifibrotics) constitute the evidence‑based, resource‑appropriate plan.

items.question:
You are an emergency medicine physician at a tertiary care center in São Paulo. A 28‑year‑old woman is brought in by ambulance after a 3‑hour wilderness hike. She reports sudden onset of severe headache, nausea, and vomiting that began shortly after she descended a steep trail. She also notes blurred vision and a sensation of “pressure” behind her eyes. She has no past medical history and is not on any medications. On arrival, vital signs are: blood pressure 150/95 mmHg, heart rate 112 bpm, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min, temperature 37.2 °C, O₂ saturation 98 % on room air. Neurologic exam reveals: alert but irritable, photophobia, bilateral papilledema on fundoscopy, and a left‑sided sixth cranial nerve palsy (inability to abduct the left eye). No focal motor deficits are noted. A non‑contrast head CT shows a hyperdense, round lesion measuring approximately 2 cm in the right posterior fossa, with surrounding edema causing mild compression of the fourth ventricle but no hydrocephalus. 

Based on this presentation, formulate:
1. The most likely diagnosis and the key clinical features that support it.
2. The immediate management steps you would take in the emergency department, including any pharmacologic and non‑pharmacologic interventions.
3. The definitive treatment options and the rationale for choosing one over the others in this clinical context.
Provide concise, evidence‑based answers suitable for an emergency physician’s rapid decision‑making.
items.answer:
**1. Most likely diagnosis** **Acute cerebellar (posterior‑fossa) intracerebral hemorrhage** – most often from a cavernous malformation or a primary hypertensive‑type bleed in a young adult without known hypertension. | Clinical clue | How it fits the diagnosis | |---------------|---------------------------| | Sudden, severe occipital/retro‑orbital headache with nausea‑vomiting | Typical for an acute intracranial bleed, especially in the posterior fossa where the tight compartment rapidly raises ICP. | | Photophobia, bilateral papilledema, left VI‑nerve palsy | Raised ICP + brain‑stem/cerebellar compression (VI palsy is a classic “false‑localising” sign). | | BP 150/95 mmHg, tachycardia | Stress‑response to pain/ICP; not enough to suggest chronic hypertension. | | Non‑contrast CT: hyperdense, round 2‑cm lesion in right cerebellum with surrounding edema, mild 4th‑ventricle compression, no hydrocephalus | Hyperdensity = acute blood; round shape = focal bleed (often cavernoma). Edema and ventricular compression = mass effect. | | Age 28, no meds, no trauma | Makes primary bleed (cavernous malformation, arteriovenous malformation rupture) more likely than hypertensive hemorrhage. | --- **2. Immediate ED management (‘‘ABCDE + ICP’’)** | Step | What to do | Rationale / Key points | |------|------------|------------------------| | **Airway & Breathing** | Keep patient supine, give 100 % O₂, monitor pulse‑oximetry. If GCS < 8 or airway compromise → rapid‑sequence intubation with cervical spine protection. | Prevent hypoxia; maintain cerebral oxygen delivery. | | **Circulation** | Two large‑bore IVs, isotonic crystalloid bolus (250 mL) if MAP < 70 mmHg. Start **nicardipine infusion** (5 mg/h, titrate to SBP < 140 mmHg, MAP > 70). | Avoid secondary ischemia; modest BP reduction reduces ongoing bleed without dropping perfusion. | | **Disability** | Quick neuro check (GCS, pupil size, extra‑ocular movements). | Baseline for serial exams; detect early deterioration. | | **Exposure/Environment** | Warm blankets, temperature control. | Prevent hypothermia, which worsens coagulopathy. | | **ICP‑targeted measures** | • **Head of bed 30°**; • **Analgesia** (IV fentanyl 25‑50 µg q5‑10 min PRN); • **Antiemetics** (ondansetron 4 mg IV); • **Osmotherapy** – **Mannitol 0.25‑1 g/kg** IV bolus *or* **3 % hypertonic saline 250 mL** over 10 min (repeat if ICP remains high). | Lower ICP rapidly; mannitol also reduces cerebral water content. | | **Steroids** | **Dexamethasone 10 mg IV** *only* if a hemorrhagic tumor is strongly suspected; otherwise avoid (no proven benefit in pure bleed). | May reduce peritumoral edema but not helpful for pure hemorrhage. | | **Coagulopathy screen** | CBC, PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, platelet function. If abnormal → reverse (vit‑K, PCC, TXA). | Even in a young healthy adult, rule out occult coagulopathy. | | **Neurosurgical activation** | Immediate bedside notification of the on‑call neurosurgeon; arrange OR availability. | Time‑critical – posterior‑fossa bleeds can herniate within hours. | | **ICP monitoring / CSF diversion** | If neurologic status worsens or hydrocephalus develops → place **external ventricular drain (EVD)** after neurosurgery consult. | Relieves obstructive hydrocephalus and provides ICP data. | | **Imaging follow‑up** | If CT was done > 30 min ago and patient deteriorates → repeat non‑contrast CT. | Detect expansion or new hydrocephalus. | --- **3. Definitive treatment options & preferred approach** | Option | Indications / Contra‑indications | Expected benefit | Why it is (or isn’t) the choice here | |--------|-----------------------------------|------------------|--------------------------------------| | **Urgent posterior‑fossa surgical evacuation** (suboccipital craniectomy ± hematoma evacuation) | • Hemorrhage ≥ 1 cm in cerebellum with mass effect **or**
• Brain‑stem compression, fourth‑ventricle obstruction, worsening neuro exam, CN VI palsy, papilledema, or ICP > 20 mmHg.
• Any clinical deterioration. | Rapid decompression → prevents tonsillar herniation, restores CSF pathways, improves mortality (≈ 30‑40 % absolute reduction vs. conservative care in symptomatic cerebellar bleeds). | **Chosen** – patient has a 2 cm bleed, edema compressing the 4th ventricle, papilledema, and a cranial‑nerve palsy → fulfills surgical criteria. | | **Conservative (ICU) management** (ICP control, blood‑pressure optimization, serial imaging) | Small (< 1 cm) bleeds, no neuro deficit, no hydrocephalus, stable ICP, patient neurologically intact. | Avoids operative risks; acceptable in selected low‑risk patients. | Not appropriate here because of size, mass effect, and focal deficits. | | **Minimally‑invasive stereotactic aspiration** | Deep‑seated supratentorial bleeds or selected cerebellar bleeds where open craniectomy is high‑risk and hematoma is liquefied. | Less invasive, quicker recovery. | Limited data for acute posterior‑fossa bleeds; does not address surrounding edema or guarantee brain‑stem decompression. | | **Endoscopic third‑ventricle or fourth‑ventricle fenestration** | Isolated obstructive hydrocephalus without large hematoma. | Relieves CSF blockage. | Not sufficient alone when the hematoma itself is causing brain‑stem compression. | | **Adjunct: EVD placement** | Hydrocephalus or uncontrolled ICP while awaiting definitive surgery. | Temporizes ICP, allows CSF drainage. | May be used pre‑/post‑op but does not replace hematoma evacuation. | **Preferred definitive plan for this patient** 1. **Urgent suboccipital craniectomy with evacuation of the cerebellar hematoma** (within the “golden 6‑hour window” when possible). 2. **Intra‑operative placement of an external ventricular drain** if intra‑operative assessment shows CSF pathway obstruction. 3. Post‑op ICU care with continued ICP monitoring, blood‑pressure goals (SBP < 140 mmHg, MAP > 70 mmHg), and early physiologic optimization (normoglycemia, euvolemia, temperature control). *Rationale*: The posterior fossa’s limited volume makes even modest hematomas life‑threatening. Early surgical decompression has the strongest evidence for reducing mortality and improving functional outcome in patients with cerebellar hemorrhage causing mass effect or neurologic decline. Conservative care carries a high risk of rapid herniation and is reserved only for truly low‑risk cases, which this patient does not meet.

items.question:
I am a pediatric neurologist in a tertiary care center in Canada, and I have a 7‑year‑old boy who presents with progressive gait instability, frequent falls, and dysarthria over the past 6 months. His MRI shows diffuse cerebellar atrophy with hyperintense lesions on T2/FLAIR in the cerebellar white matter, but no contrast enhancement. Laboratory workup reveals normal serum lactate, ammonia, and metabolic panel; CSF analysis is unremarkable. The family reports a history of a cousin with a similar presentation who was diagnosed with a mitochondrial disorder in early adolescence.

What are the key differential diagnoses to consider in this child, and which specific clinical features, imaging findings, and targeted laboratory or genetic tests would help differentiate between:

1. Autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxia (e.g., Friedreich ataxia, ataxia‑telangiectasia, SCARs)?
2. Mitochondrial cerebellar ataxia (e.g., POLG‑related disease, mitochondrial encephalomyopathy)?
3. Non‑genetic causes (e.g., post‑infectious cerebellitis, autoimmune cerebellar ataxia)?

Please outline a step‑wise diagnostic algorithm, including recommended first‑line and second‑line investigations, and indicate which findings would most strongly point toward each category.
items.answer:
**Pediatric Cerebellar Ataxia – 7‑yr‑old boy** *Key problem*: Progressive gait instability, falls and dysarthria over 6 months; MRI = diffuse cerebellar atrophy + T2/FLAIR white‑matter hyperintensities, no gadolinium enhancement. Routine metabolic work‑up is normal. A cousin with a “mitochondrial disorder” raises the possibility of an inherited metabolic disease, but the phenotype could also fit a classic hereditary ataxia or an acquired/post‑infectious process. Below is a **concise, practical guide** for a tertiary‑care neurologist in Canada (or any centre with access to a genetics/metabolic service). It is organized into three diagnostic blocks, the clinical/ radiologic clues that favour each block, and the **step‑wise algorithm** (first‑line → second‑line → definitive testing). --- ## 1. Differential Diagnosis – “Broad Categories” | Category | Representative disorders (examples) | Typical age of onset | Key clinical “red‑flags” that tip the balance toward this group | |----------|--------------------------------------|----------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------| | **A. Autosomal‑recessive cerebellar ataxias (AR‑CA)** | • Friedreich ataxia (FXN)
• Ataxia‑telangiectasia (ATM)
• SCAR (e.g., **SACS**, **SETX**, **ANO10**, **TDP2**, **PNKP**, **TTC19**, **VPS13C**, **CAPN1**, **SYNE1**, **CABC1**, **PCH** genes) | 1–10 yr (most) or adolescence (some SCAR) | • Progressive gait ataxia + loss of deep tendon reflexes (FRDA)
• Oculocutaneous telangiectasias, immunodeficiency, ↑α‑fetoprotein (A‑T)
• Early‑onset severe cerebellar atrophy + spasticity, peripheral neuropathy, cataracts (ARSACS)
• Consanguinity, multiple affected siblings, recessive pedigree | | **B. Mitochondrial cerebellar ataxias** | • POLG‑related disease (Alpers‑type, ataxia‑myopathy, progressive external ophthalmoplegia)
• mtDNA point‑mutations (e.g., m.3243A>G, m.8344A>G)
• mtDNA deletions (Kearns‑Sayre, chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia)
• Nuclear‑encoded mitochondrial disease (e.g., C10orf2/TWNK, NDUFAF2, COQ8A) | Variable (infancy–adolescence) | • Multisystem involvement (myopathy, sensorineural hearing loss, optic atrophy, diabetes, cardiomyopathy, liver dysfunction)
• Episodic worsening after stress/fasting
• Elevated lactate in serum/CSF (often, but can be normal)
• Family history compatible with maternal inheritance or autosomal recessive (if nuclear) | | **C. Non‑genetic / acquired cerebellar ataxia** | • Post‑infectious cerebellitis (post‑viral, post‑vaccinal)
• Autoimmune cerebellar ataxia (anti‑GAD, anti‑Yo, anti‑Hu, anti‑Tr, anti‑VKH, anti‑mGluR1, anti‑DPPX)
• Paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration (rare in children)
• Toxic (e.g., alcohol, phenytoin, heavy metals)
• Structural lesions (posterior fossa tumor, vascular malformation) | Acute–sub‑acute (days‑weeks) for post‑infectious; sub‑acute (weeks‑months) for autoimmune; chronic progressive for toxins/tumor | • Recent viral illness, vaccination, or drug exposure
• Rapid onset (days‑weeks) with cerebellar edema on MRI (often contrast‑enhancing)
• Presence of other autoimmune features (dermatitis, thyroiditis)
• Positive neuronal antibodies in serum/CSF
• Normal family history; sporadic case | --- ## 2. + seizures + liver failure (possible) | Cerebellar atrophy + basal ganglia stroke‑like lesions | ↑ lactate (often) | POLG sequencing (panel) | | mtDNA point mutation (m.3243A>G) | Maternal | Diabetes,
